patterns.name: Chat citation and link artifacts
patterns.summary: Machine traces that a chat assistant adds to sources survive copy and paste: links carry the tracking parameter "utm_source=chatgpt.com" or "utm_source=openai", and citation tokens of the interface such as ":contentReference[oaicite:2]{index=2}" or a bare "oaicite" appear in the text or in reference URLs. They show that links or passages were taken from a chat answer without editing, and in reference lists they often mark sources nobody opened.

positive: Source: https://www.example.org/reports/2026-outlook?utm_source=chatgpt.com
The agency revised its forecast in March. :contentReference[oaicite:2]{index=2}
See the filing guidance (https://www.example.gov/pub/guide.pdf?utm_source=openai) for details.
Enrollment grew by 12 percent after the policy change contentReference[oaicite:1].
negative: Read the launch post at https://shop.example.com/blog?utm_source=newsletter&utm_medium=email.
In GA4, filter the session source for chatgpt.com to see referrals from ChatGPT.
The utm_source parameter tells the analytics tool which site sent the visitor.
OpenAI published the citation guidelines for its search product in a help-center article.

patterns.legitimate_use: Analytics and SEO writing explains these parameters, and reporting on AI misuse quotes them; such texts discuss the strings rather than carry them in their own links. A link copied from a chat answer can still point to a real, checked source: the parameter shows the path the link took, not that the surrounding prose was generated, so treat a hit as a prompt to verify the citations.
patterns.fix: Remove the tracking parameter from every URL and delete the citation tokens. Open each cited source, confirm that it exists and supports the claim, and replace the link with a clean, canonical URL or a proper reference.
patterns.prevention: Never paste links or citations from a chat answer unchecked. Strip tracking parameters and interface tokens, and cite only sources you have opened.
patterns.notes: Mechanism: technical residue of the chat interface's source handling, not a style choice. Closest existing pattern: format-bleed (unrendered markdown such as asterisks, hash signs or pipe tables). Markdown is a general markup language that any writer may use; these strings are generated by one product's citation and link tracking and have no human use in running text. The Wikipedia guide notes that other assistants add their own referrer parameters; only the ChatGPT strings read in the sources are in the detector. Bloomberg Law reports that ChatGPT may append the parameter to links it provides, and the Originality.ai study reports that the tag occurs on some, not all, of its links, so its absence proves nothing.

sources.note: ChatGPT "may add utm_source=openai or utm_source=chatgpt.com" to source URLs; exposed internal citation markup such as contentReference[oaicite:1] is called a more unambiguous sign. The guide adds that the parameter shows tool involvement, not that the writing is generated.
utm_source=chatgpt.com found in four federal court opinions and three government documents.
44 SEC filing documents from January to June 2026 contained utm_source=chatgpt.com.
Relays the Washington Post finding that some citations of a May 2025 government report included "oaicite" in their URLs.

patterns.name: Compulsive counting
patterns.summary: The text announces the exact number of items before or inside a list ("Five things we wish to discuss", "Here are the top seven"), as if getting the count right were itself the achievement. The number adds nothing, and the list that follows often does not justify it.

positive: Five things we wish to discuss today.
Four reasons why this will work.
Three key takeaways from the conference:
Here are the top seven tools for remote teams.
negative: There are two ways to install the package: with pip or from source.
We tested five strategies against a control group of 120 patients.
Three people were injured when the scaffold collapsed.
The top seven floors of the tower are offices.

positive: Fünf Dinge, die wir heute besprechen wollen.
Vier Gründe, warum das funktioniert.
Drei zentrale Erkenntnisse aus der Konferenz:
Hier sind die sieben wichtigsten Tipps für Teams im Homeoffice.
negative: Es gibt zwei Wege, das Paket zu installieren: mit pip oder aus dem Quellcode.
Wir haben fünf Strategien an 120 Patienten getestet.
Drei Personen wurden bei dem Unfall verletzt.
Die oberen sieben Etagen sind Büros.

patterns.legitimate_use: A count is information when the reader needs it: a checklist with a fixed number of steps, a title promising a set the text then delivers, or a legal text with numbered grounds. Dismiss a hit when the number lets the reader track progress or verify completeness; flag counts that only announce a list.
patterns.fix: Drop the number and introduce the content directly, or make the items carry the structure themselves. Use a numbered list only for items that are truly parallel.
patterns.prevention: Do not announce the number of points before listing them ("Here are five reasons"). Present the points; let the reader count if it matters.
patterns.notes: tropes-fyi and skill-avoid-ai-writing (registered as derived from it) form one independence cluster under docs/architecture.md section 5.2; popularai-ai-tells-2026 is a second, independent cluster. Counts below three are left out of the detector because "two ways" or "two options" is usually informative. No source gives a quantified threshold. Demarcation: triad is the three-part figure itself; this pattern announces a count of any size in advance.

Comparable examples and the fix rule to use numbered lists only for real parallelism.

patterns.name: Compulsive summary
patterns.summary: A formulaic opening of the closing paragraph ("In summary", "Overall", "In conclusion", "Zusammenfassend lässt sich sagen") that introduces a coda restating what the text has already said.

positive: In conclusion, the migration was a success.
In summary, the options differ mainly in cost.
Overall, the new process saves time and money.
All in all, it was a productive quarter.
We fixed the cache and the queue. At the end of the day, what matters is the customer.
negative: Overall latency dropped from 210 ms to 140 ms after the cache change.
The summary table lists all 14 endpoints.
In summary statistics, the median is more stable than the mean.
Ultimate frisbee practice moves to Thursday.

positive: Zusammenfassend lässt sich sagen, dass die Migration erfolgreich war.
Insgesamt zeigt sich, dass die Optionen sich vor allem im Preis unterscheiden.
Abschließend ist festzuhalten, dass das Projekt im Zeitplan liegt.
Alles in allem war es ein produktives Quartal.
Wir haben Cache und Queue repariert. Unterm Strich zählt der Kunde.
negative: Insgesamt wurden 42 Proben analysiert.
Die Zusammenfassung steht auf Seite 2.
Abschließend wurde der Server neu gestartet und der Test wiederholt.
Unterm Tisch lag das fehlende Kabel.

patterns.legitimate_use: Long reports and theses often need an explicitly labelled conclusion; a heading such as "Conclusion" or "Fazit" is not the pattern. A closing sentence that adds a new consequence or a concrete next step is fine even when it starts with "Overall". Flag the formula when the last paragraph only restates what the text already said.
patterns.fix: Delete the summary formula. If the text does not hold up without a coda, fix the argument instead and end on the last new piece of information or on the concrete next step.
patterns.prevention: Do not end with a paragraph that opens with "In conclusion", "In summary", "Overall" or "Zusammenfassend lässt sich sagen". End on the last new point.

sources.note: Advises deleting the summary sentence at the end.

patterns.name: Concession pivot
patterns.summary: An objection is granted in passing and immediately turned into a positive or neutral verdict without any engagement with the objection itself ("Despite its challenges, X remains promising", "Trotz dieser Herausforderungen bleibt X vielversprechend"). The false-balance close ("the truth lies somewhere in between") belongs to the same formula.

positive: Despite its challenges, the project remains promising.
Despite these challenges, the initiative continues to thrive.
While the framework has limitations, it's still remarkable.
Critics argue it is too slow, supporters say it is safer. The truth lies somewhere in between.
Both approaches have their merits.
negative: Despite the outage, the team shipped the release on Friday.
Despite these limitations, we report results only for the English subset.
While the tool has limitations, they are listed in the README with workarounds.
Both sides have filed motions, which the court will hear on 3 June.

positive: Trotz dieser Herausforderungen bleibt das Projekt vielversprechend.
Trotz aller Schwierigkeiten ist die Initiative weiterhin auf Erfolgskurs.
Auch wenn das Tool seine Grenzen hat, ist es dennoch bemerkenswert.
Kritiker halten es für zu langsam, Befürworter für sicherer. Die Wahrheit liegt wie so oft in der Mitte.
Beide Ansätze haben ihre Berechtigung.
negative: Trotz der Störung wurde das Release am Freitag ausgeliefert.
Trotz dieser Einschränkungen sind die Ergebnisse nur für den deutschen Teil gültig.
Obwohl das Tool Grenzen hat, sind sie im README mit Workarounds dokumentiert.
Beide Seiten haben Klage eingereicht; das Gericht verhandelt am 3. Juni.

patterns.legitimate_use: A concession that is actually weighed is fine: the objection is named concretely and the verdict follows from evidence ("Despite the 40 % higher cost we kept vendor A, because a migration would take nine months"). Limitation paragraphs in research papers that list concrete limits and then state, with numbers, what still holds are also fine. Flag the formula when the objection stays vague ("its challenges") and the turn to a positive or neutral verdict comes without an argument.
patterns.fix: Name the objection concretely and weigh it, or delete both the concession and the verdict. If the honest answer is mixed, say with evidence what each side gets right instead of placing the truth in the middle.
patterns.prevention: Do not wave off objections with "despite these challenges" or "while it has limitations, it remains...". Either name the specific objection and answer it with evidence, or leave it out.

sources.note: A Substack field guide to AI tells ("I Asked the Machine to Tell on Itself", 2026-04-24, entry "False Concession") describes the same formula; it is not registered as a source.

patterns.name: Contraction avoidance
patterns.summary: English text in an informal setting consistently avoids contractions ("I am not sure we are ready, but it is worth a try") and uses stiff, formal phrasing where a person would write "I'm", "we're", "it's" and "don't". The register mismatch makes chat replies, posts and personal emails sound like documentation.

positive: I am not sure we are ready, but it is worth a try.
Do not worry, you will love it.
We cannot make it tonight, sorry!
negative: I'm not sure we're ready, but it's worth a try.
Don't forget the cables; we can't start without them.
The cannon fired at noon.
Isn't it late already?

patterns.legitimate_use: Formal registers (legal, academic, official correspondence, documentation) avoid contractions by convention, and writers use the full form for emphasis ("I do not agree"). The pattern only matters in informal texts such as chat replies, social posts and personal emails.
patterns.fix: In informal texts, contract auxiliaries and pronouns the way people speak ("I'm", "it's", "don't"), and keep full forms only for emphasis.
patterns.prevention: Match the register: use contractions in informal English writing, and full forms only where the context is formal or the emphasis is intended.
patterns.notes: Independent sources: the Pangram guide, the ACL 2025 expert-annotator study (russell-acl-2025-expert-detectors), a corpus study of argumentative essays (alghazo-eujal-2026-informality) and the Reuters Institute; jetwong-neocities compiles other lists, among them the Wikipedia guide. Counter-evidence: o1-Pro used contractions freely enough to mislead an expert annotator, so newer reasoning models may not show the pattern. English only: German has no comparable contraction system (forms such as "gibt's" are optional in most registers). The engine cannot switch the pattern off outside informal context, so the default threshold of 4 full forms per 100 words is set high and the informal override at 2 per 100 words; neither is calibrated against the reference corpora yet. Expected false positives in formal texts, which the default threshold only partly prevents. The detector counts full forms; it cannot verify that contractions are absent.

sources.note: Consistent avoidance of contractions and stiff phrasing in contexts that are actually informal.
AI text "rarely uses contractions like 'we've'" and "writes in an extremely formal tone unless it instructed not to". Qualitative.

12.3 % of expert explanations cite formality: AI text "rarely contains filler words, contractions, slang, or abbreviations, favoring fully spelled-out terms and a polished tone". The same paper reports that o1-Pro's frequent contractions and colloquialisms misled one annotator.

40 ChatGPT essays vs. 40 LOCNESS student essays: the AI essays avoid "most conversational elements such as contractions, second-person pronouns, and fragments"; chi-square differences significant for nearly all 12 informality markers. Academic register; abstract read only.

Linguist Karolina Rudnicka: when asked to review drafts, ChatGPT and Grammarly "also avoid slang, contractions (like 'gonna' and 'wanna'), colloquial language and passive voice". Qualitative, about revision rather than free generation, and the examples are colloquial rather than standard contractions.

patterns.name: Copula avoidance
patterns.summary: A plain "is", "are" or "has" is replaced by a more elaborate verb: the gallery "serves as" the city's venue, the bridge "stands as" a reminder, the hotel "boasts" 200 rooms, the school "holds the distinction of being" the oldest. The substitute verbs add a note of function, monument or pride that the facts do not carry, and repeated across a text they make plain description sound like a brochure or a plaque.

positive: The gallery serves as the city's main venue for contemporary art.
Today the bridge stands as a reminder of the region's industrial past.
The hotel boasts over 200 rooms and a rooftop pool.
The school holds the distinction of being the oldest in the county.
The square serves as a gathering place, and the old town hall stands as a symbol of civic pride.
negative: The gallery is the city's main venue for contemporary art.
She served as a senator from 2004 to 2010.
He stands as the Green Party candidate in the northern ward.
The protein functions as a receptor for the hormone.
The town boasted of its new library for years.

patterns.legitimate_use: "Serves as" is precise when something takes on a role it does not normally have ("the gym serves as an emergency shelter"), and "stands as a candidate" is standard British usage. Technical writing uses "serves as" for components with a defined role. Flag the verbs when they replace "is" or "has" in plain description, especially when several appear in one text.
patterns.fix: Use "is", "are" or "has" unless the elaborate verb says something the copula does not: "The gallery is the city's main venue", "The hotel has 200 rooms". If the point is a role or a symbol, state who uses it that way and how.
patterns.prevention: Prefer "is", "are" and "has" for description. Use "serves as" only for a role something does not normally have, and never use "boasts" or "stands as" for neutral facts.
patterns.notes: Mechanism: avoidance of the basic copula in favor of verbs with built-in emphasis. Closest existing patterns: inflated-importance (significance framing such as "stands as a testament to", "marks a pivotal moment") and brochure-tone (promotional adjectives). This pattern concerns the verb slot in ordinary description and fires on "serves as the main venue" or "boasts 200 rooms", which state no significance; "stands as a testament to" hits both patterns. Past-tense "served as" is left out because it reports offices held ("served as a senator"), and "functions as" and "represents" because they are standard in science writing. Threshold 2 per text, since one "serves as" is ordinary. Independence: the Wikipedia guide cites the Geng and Trotta decline of "is" and "are" in its section, but its entry rests on its own dated examples, and the study's frequency data do not depend on the guide, so the two count as separate lines of evidence. tropes-fyi reuses the guide's "Gallery 825" example and gptzero-ai-patterns states that its taxonomy is derived from the guide; neither is counted as independent here.

patterns.name: Curly quotes in plain text
patterns.summary: Typographic (curly) quotation marks and apostrophes in plain-text contexts, typically carried over by copy and paste from an interface that renders them. Kept apart from em dash density so that the two typography signals are measured separately.

positive: The memo called it “a turning point” for the team.
She answered ‘no’ twice before the vote.
It’s ready for review.
negative: The memo called it "a turning point" for the team.
She answered 'no' twice before the vote.
Er nannte es »einen Wendepunkt« und ging.
„Das ist nicht die Lösung, die wir brauchen“, sagte die Leiterin und verwies auf die Messwerte aus dem Juni.

patterns.legitimate_use: Word processors and phone keyboards insert curly quotes and apostrophes automatically, and typeset publications use them by design. German („…“, ‚…‘) is exempt, and other languages with their own quotation conventions deserve the same treatment. Treat a hit as an artifact signal only in plain-text channels such as commit messages or Markdown files, where writers normally type straight quotes.
patterns.fix: Convert curly quotes and apostrophes to straight ones in plain-text channels.
patterns.prevention: In plain-text channels use straight quotes (" and ') unless the target language or the publication style requires typographic quotes.
patterns.notes: Observation, not scored. Any curly quote or apostrophe counts; the metric also counts U+2019 used as an apostrophe. The fix — finally — landed on Friday. It was small — three lines — but it closed the oldest bug in the tracker. The bug had been open since the first public release and showed up only when two users saved the same draft within one second. Support had collected more than forty reports over the years, most of them from teams that share a single account. The patch adds a version check before each save and rejects the second write with a clear message. We ran the full test suite on three platforms and added two new tests for the race. The release notes describe the change and link to the original report.

The new release changes how the scheduler assigns jobs to workers. Until now every job went to the first idle worker, which caused uneven load when long exports and short thumbnail jobs arrived at the same time. The scheduler now estimates the run time of each job from the last fifty runs of the same type and places it on the worker with the lowest expected finish time. In our staging cluster this cut the p95 queue wait from 41 seconds to 12 seconds over a two week test. Memory use on the coordinator grew by about 30 MB, which is within the budget for the current hardware. The estimate falls back to the old behaviour when fewer than ten historical runs exist, so new job types are not delayed by missing data. Operators can switch the feature off with a single flag in the config file — the default is on for all clusters created after version 4.2. Existing clusters keep the old behaviour until the flag is set by hand during the next maintenance window, and the release notes describe the change with examples for both cases.

patterns.legitimate_use: Fiction and typeset publications use dashes as a deliberate style. German uses the spaced en dash as its standard Gedankenstrich, which the metric counts as well. patterns.prevention: Use dashes sparingly, at most a few per 500 words. Prefer other punctuation or a new sentence.
patterns.notes: Threshold set so that at most 4 % of the human reference corpus (pre-2022 texts, de and en) triggers it; separation from AI-generated text is not yet measured. The threshold of more than 5.25 per 500 words (10.5 per 1,000) sits at the upper end of the human range that SlopDetector reports (up to about 10 per 1,000). The rule applies to all registers, not only to expository prose. Because density is computed per 500 words, two dashes trigger in texts shorter than about 190 words; below 100 words of analyzed text the short-text rule keeps the pattern from triggering, because one or two dashes there say nothing about density. Texts of more than 150 words are unaffected. Given the model dependence, a hit is best weighed together with other accumulation signals; this is not encoded as requires. Curly quotes are covered by curly-quotes.

patterns.name: False agency
patterns.summary: Inanimate or abstract entities (data, tools, decisions, cultures, complaints) appear as actors that tell or choose things, or that change on their own ("the data tells a story", "the tool chose to focus", "complaints become fixes"). The phrasing hides the person or institution that acted.

detector.rubric: Flag clauses whose grammatical subject is an inanimate or abstract entity (data, a tool, a decision, a culture, a market, complaints, a strategy, a document) combined with a verb that presupposes intention, perception, speech or choice (tells, chooses, decides, wants, knows, believes, insists) or with a self-causing change (the decision emerged, complaints become fixes, cultures shift), where the sentence thereby hides the person or institution who acted. Count each such clause once. Do not flag conventional descriptions of mechanical behavior (a function returns a value, a sensor measures, a valve opens, a thermostat switches), institutions acting through their members (the board decided, the court ruled), established citation metonymy (the study found, the report lists), or deliberate personification in fiction and poetry. In code descriptions, flag only the anthropomorphic verb: in "is_file() swallows that and returns False", "swallows" counts and "returns" does not.

patterns.name: Forced figurative language

detector.rubric: Find similes and metaphors that are strained or coined for effect and do not make the point clearer than a literal statement would. Do not count idioms and dead metaphors used as ordinary vocabulary (bottleneck, pipeline, Engpass, Flaschenhals), images that make an abstract or technical idea concrete for the reader, figurative language in fiction, poetry or advertising slogans, and quoted speech. Return each strained image as a hit.

patterns.name: Format bleed
patterns.summary: Markdown syntax that was never rendered shows up literally in the final text: asterisks around words, hash signs in front of headings, backticks, pipe tables or bracketed link syntax in an email, a chat message, a form field or a printed letter. It is a technical artifact of pasting generated output into a medium that does not render markdown.

detector.rubric: Decide from the text itself whether its target medium renders markdown. Signals for plain text: email greeting and sign-off, letter layout, SMS or chat style, form-field answers, subtitles, social posts on platforms without markdown. Only for such texts, find literal markdown syntax that a reader would see as stray characters: **bold** or __bold__ markers, single asterisks or underscores used for italics, lines starting with #, ##, ###, backtick code spans or fences, pipe-table rows, [text](url) links, and escaped markers such as \*. Do not count markdown in documents meant for rendering (README files, wiki pages, chat platforms that render markdown), asterisks used as footnote markers or censoring (f***), hashtags in social posts, and code samples. Return each stray markup span as a hit.

patterns.name: Dramatic fragment pathos
patterns.summary: Incomplete or extremely clipped sentences at the end of a paragraph or text that simulate emotional weight or finality ("That's it. That's the whole thing.", "The future isn't coming. It's already here."). Inside running text the same device is a legitimate stylistic sharpening; only the closing position counts.

detector.rubric: Inspect only the final one or two sentences of each paragraph and of the whole text. Report a hit when they are incomplete or extremely short sentences (usually under six words, often verbless, a bare noun phrase, or a set-up and punchline pair) whose function is to create emotional weight or finality instead of adding information. Typical shapes: "That's it. That's the whole thing.", "X isn't coming. It's already here.", "Every. Single. Time.", "And that changes everything.", "Let that sink in.", "Das war's. Mehr nicht.", "Sie ist längst da." Do not report fragments in the middle of a paragraph. Do not report short closing sentences that carry information, for example a number or an instruction ("See Table 2.", "Restart the service."). Ignore quoted dialogue. Ignore headings and captions. Report at most one hit per paragraph ending and quote the fragment or fragments.

patterns.name: Function-word shift
patterns.summary: A cluster of prepositions and conjunctions becomes more frequent in LLM-assisted English prose: "across", "into", "where", "while" and "beyond" ("insights across teams", "beyond the dashboard", "while ensuring"). Each word is ordinary; the shift shows only as a density change across a text.

positive: We rolled the tool out across all teams, beyond the original pilot group.
The model turns raw logs into insights while keeping costs low.
This is where the new workflow helps.
negative: Meanwhile, the team moved the servers to the new data center in May.
Whereas the old process took days, the new one takes an hour.

patterns.legitimate_use: These are high-frequency function words; any single use is normal. Only an unusual density over a longer text is of interest, and even then technical descriptions of spatial or temporal relations use them legitimately.
patterns.fix: Check whether "across", "beyond" and "while" carry a literal relation of place or time. Replace vague uses with the concrete relation ("in all three teams", "in addition to").
patterns.prevention: Use "across", "beyond", "into", "where" and "while" only for their literal relation; prefer the concrete phrasing when the relation is vague.
patterns.notes: Both sources are arXiv preprints on academic registers. They count as two clusters under docs/architecture.md section 5.2 (academic sources cluster by shared authors), but kobak-excess-vocabulary corroborates only "across", and no known source describes the shift as a nameable trope with example sentences, so the pattern stays an observation. English only, so there is no German realization; German equivalents have no evidence yet. The density threshold of 12 per 1,000 words is not calibrated against the reference corpora and is expected to misfire on many ordinary English texts; it exists to let a measurement test the claim. The core phrases are "nicht nur X, sondern auch Y" (when repeated), "eine zentrale Rolle spielen", "das volle Potenzial ausschöpfen" and unnatural compound chains. Below the threshold, hits never count as a finding. When the text already shows a strong accumulation of other findings, they may be listed as a supplementary note without weight. Judge each hit by whether a more specific verb or noun would say what actually happens.
patterns.fix: Replace each word with a verb or noun that names the actual process or object ("delve into the data" becomes "compare the March and April logs").

patterns.notes: Below the threshold, hits never count as a finding. When the text already shows a strong accumulation of other findings, they may be listed as a supplementary note without weight. patterns.name: Hollow sentences (deletion test)
patterns.summary: Sentences sound self-contained and quotable yet carry no concrete, checkable statement: no number, name, date or fact. Deleting them in thought leaves the reader with the same information. When more than a third of a text's sentences pass this deletion test, the text is padded with pseudo-substance.

detector.rubric: Apply a deletion test to every sentence of the text. A sentence is hollow when deleting it would leave the reader with the same information: it contains no concrete, checkable content (no number, name, date, place, quantity, specific event, definition, instruction, or claim specific enough that someone could dispute it) and it supplies no reason, condition or logical step that a neighboring sentence depends on. Typical forms are quotable one-liners, pseudo-wisdom, generic praise and closing lines that restate the mood of the paragraph. Skip headings, list labels, questions that set up a following answer, quoted speech, and sentences in fiction or poetry. A topic sentence counts as hollow only if the paragraph states the same point concretely and the topic sentence adds nothing to it. Return each hollow sentence as a hit and report value = number of hollow sentences divided by the number of sentences evaluated.

patterns.name: "Hope this finds you well" opener
patterns.summary: An email or letter opens with the stock well-wishing line "I hope this email finds you well" or a close variant ("Hope this message finds you well", "I trust this note finds you in good health"). Writing assistants default to it, so the line now reads as template; it delays the reason for writing and could open any email to anyone.

positive:
Dear Dr. Chen,

I hope this email finds you well. I am writing to ask about openings in your lab.
Hi Sam, hope this finds you well! Quick question about the invoice.
I trust this message finds you in good health.
Hello team, I hope my note finds you well after the long weekend.
negative: I hope the move to Leeds went well and the boxes are unpacked.
I hope you had a good weekend at the coast.
This tool finds you the cheapest flights well before peak season.
I hope this email reaches the right team; the form on your site kept failing.

patterns.legitimate_use: The line is an established courtesy in formal correspondence, and in some business cultures and varieties of English (for example Indian English) it is the expected opening. Flag it where it is the only opening content or appears in cold outreach and generated drafts; do not treat a single formal letter that uses it as evidence on its own.
patterns.fix: Open with the reason for writing, or with a well-wish that is specific to the recipient ("I hope the launch went smoothly").
patterns.prevention: Do not open emails with "I hope this email finds you well" or its variants. State the purpose in the first sentence.
patterns.notes: Mechanism: a fixed salutation formula in the first lines of an email. Closest existing patterns: sycophant-residue (chat politeness addressed to the user, such as "I hope this helps!") and generic-opening (openers that frame the present age or announce the text). This formula addresses the email recipient and is a genre convention that writing assistants now produce by default. Expected false positives: human formal email, where the phrase predates chat assistants; the gate measures how far it separates the two. Both sources are vendor blogs without data.

patterns.name: "Imagine a world" invitation
patterns.summary: A sentence invites the reader to imagine an ideal state ("Imagine a world where every tool you use talks to the others", "Imagine never having to chase an invoice again", "Imagine if your team could ship in hours") and then lists the outcomes the product or idea promises. The hypothetical pitch replaces a description of what the thing does today and asks the reader to grant the premise before any evidence.

positive: Imagine a world where every tool you use talks to every other tool.
Imagine never having to chase an unpaid invoice again.
Imagine if your team could ship features in hours instead of weeks.

negative: I can't imagine a world where the tax code gets simpler.
Imagine Dragons played two encores at the stadium.

John Lennon released "Imagine" in 1971.

patterns.legitimate_use: Thought experiments, puzzles and teaching examples ask the reader to imagine a precisely defined situation ("Imagine the cube rotated 90 degrees"), and fiction or speeches may use the invitation once on purpose. Flag the open-ended "imagine a world where / imagine if your ..." pitch in marketing, product and opinion prose.
patterns.fix: Replace the hypothetical with what the product or idea does now, for whom, and with what measured result. If the future state matters, state it as a claim with the conditions it depends on.
patterns.prevention: Do not open with "Imagine a world where" or "Imagine if". Describe the current situation and the concrete change.
patterns.notes: Mechanism: a second-person invitation to an idealized hypothetical that frames the pitch. Closest existing patterns: generic-opening ("In today's fast-paced world", "In a world where"), which frames the present age, and false-range ("from startups to Fortune 500s"). This pattern invites the reader into an imagined future instead of describing the present; it is not limited to the text start. "I can't imagine a world where" and similar first-person uses are excluded by requiring "Imagine" at sentence start. tropes.fyi rates the entry as fading. Single-source observation.

patterns.name: Invented concept label
patterns.summary: The text coins a catchy, analytical-sounding term for its own point and then treats it as an established concept: an abstract problem noun (paradox, trap, creep, tax, divide, inversion) is attached to a domain word ("the supervision paradox", "the acceleration trap", "workload creep"), often introduced with "call it ..." or "nennen wir es ...", and never defined or attributed. Several such labels in one piece borrow the authority of a field vocabulary that does not exist.

detector.rubric: Find compound labels that the text coins for its own argument and presents as if they were established terms. Typical shape: an abstract problem noun (paradox, trap, creep, tax, gap, divide, inversion, problem, loop, spiral, cliff, debt; German Paradox, Falle, Steuer, Lücke, Kluft, Schere, Spirale) attached to a domain word, sometimes introduced by "call it", "let's call this", "what I call", "nennen wir es", "man könnte es ... nennen". Count a label only if the text neither defines it with checkable criteria nor attributes it to a source, and if it is not an established term of the field (for example scope creep, feature creep, digital divide, liquidity trap, poverty trap, technical debt, priority inversion, dependency inversion, birthday paradox, Fachkräftemangel, Liquiditätsfalle). Do not count product names, named metrics the text defines and measures, or quoted terms from other authors. Each distinct label counts once, however often it recurs. Return each coined label as a hit with the sentence in which it first appears.

patterns.legitimate_use: Essays and research papers may introduce one new term on purpose, define it, and use it consistently as a handle for a concept the text develops. Established terms of a field and attributed concepts are no finding. Flag labels that appear without definition, often several per text, and that a plain description would replace without loss.
patterns.fix: Replace the label with a plain description of the mechanism it stands for. If the concept is needed throughout the text, define it once with concrete criteria and keep it.
patterns.prevention: Do not coin catchy labels such as "the X paradox" or "the Y trap" for your own points. Describe the mechanism in plain words, or use the established term of the field.

patterns.fix: Remove emphasis that does not mark something the reader must not miss; keep at most one emphasis per paragraph. Drop headings from short texts, and strip markdown entirely where it will not be rendered.
patterns.prevention: Use bold, italics and headings only where they help the reader find or not miss something. Write plain text for emails, chat replies and other media that do not render markdown.
patterns.notes: No source gives a per-text threshold (Pangram reports frequency multiples). patterns.prevention: Do not open with assistant framing such as "Certainly! Here's", "Below is a summary" or "Let me walk you through". Start with the content itself.

patterns.legitimate_use: Academic writing and legal texts use nominal style by convention; the threshold is switched off for the academic context. Lexicalized nouns ("information", "government", "Zeitung", "Wohnung") and verbs that happen to end in a listed suffix ("implement") are suffix matches without stylistic weight; the host model should discount them.
patterns.fix: Turn nominalizations back into verbs with a named subject ("wir operationalisieren" instead of "die Durchführung der Operationalisierung"; "we optimize" instead of "the implementation of the optimization").
patterns.prevention: Prefer verbs with a named actor over nouns derived from verbs (-ung, -heit, -keit, -tion in German; -tion, -ment, -ness, -ity in English), especially outside academic writing.
patterns.notes: Threshold set so that at most 4 % of the human reference corpus (pre-2022 texts, de and en) triggers it; separation from AI-generated text is not yet measured. Suffix tokens are common in ordinary prose: the median human text has about 8 per 300 words, and at 3 per 300 words 85 % (de) and 87 % (en) of the human texts triggered. The threshold of 23 per 300 words (about one word in thirteen) marks the densest 4 % of human texts in both languages. The reference corpus holds texts of 150 words and more; in very short texts two or three nominalizations already exceed the density, so the short-text rule requires at least 100 words of analyzed text (a 22-word sentence pair with "communication" and "connections" reached 27.3 per 300 words). Texts of more than 150 words are unaffected. The academic override uses a value above the window size (more than 300 per 300 words) because the threshold object has no explicit off switch. The parameter names suffixes (per language) and min_word_length are specific to this metric; the architecture only states that the suffix list lives in params. This pattern covers verbs turned into nouns; premodifier-stacking covers modification moved into the noun phrase and stacked-nouns covers noun-noun compound chains.

patterns.prevention: Do not announce a point before making it ("Here's the kicker", "But here's the thing", "Was die wenigsten wissen:"). Make the point.

sources.note: In explicitly informal short formats (e.g. social media posts) a single announcement is tolerated; encoded as the informal context override.

patterns.name: Premise stacking
patterns.summary: Supporting statements pile up ahead of the point, often ahead of a question, so that by the time the point arrives it has already been made two or three times. The reader works through preparation that the conclusion then repeats ("Now imagine if this was simply: Is next-day delivery available in this region?").

detector.rubric: Find passages where two or more sentences of setup or evidence precede a point (a claim, a recommendation or a question) and that point merely restates what the setup has already made clear. Count a passage when deleting the final point, or deleting most of the setup, would lose no information. Do not count arguments in which each premise adds a distinct step that the conclusion needs, worked examples, legal or mathematical reasoning, and stories that build toward an outcome the reader cannot predict. Return each stacked passage as a hit, quoting the point it leads up to.

positive: Customers want to know whether they can get their order tomorrow. They search for it on the product page. They ask support about it every day. Now imagine if this was simply: Is next-day delivery available in this region?

patterns.legitimate_use: Technical and legal writing relies on established compound modifiers ("open-source license", "real-time system", "end-to-end test", "long-term contract"); one or two per paragraph are normal. patterns.prevention: Avoid stacking hyphenated or participial modifiers in front of nouns. Prefer a relative clause or a short sentence that names the actor.
patterns.notes: No source gives a threshold. The value of more than 2 hyphenated premodifiers per 100 words is not yet calibrated against the reference corpora. patterns.legitimate_use: Plain-language writing, children's books, instructions and spoken-style texts use short, simple sentences with few commas on purpose. Some authors chain clauses with "and" for rhythm (polysyndeton). Dismiss a hit when the sentences are short or the and-chain is a deliberate stylistic choice; flag long sentences whose clauses are strung together without structure.
patterns.fix: Split overlong and-chains into separate sentences, or subordinate the less important clause (because, although, which). Use commas, semicolons or parentheses where they mark the logic of the sentence.
patterns.prevention: Do not chain three or more clauses with "and" in one sentence. Break long sentences, and use punctuation to show which part depends on which.
patterns.notes: No source gives an operational threshold; the closest operationalization of the evidence would count commas and semicolons per 100 words. The registry metric comma_density counts commas per sentence, so the value 0.4 with at least 8 sentences is a proxy and not yet calibrated against the reference corpora. The and-stacking component is not covered by the metric; a host model applying the pattern by hand should check it. patterns.name: Reader-directed emphasis command
patterns.summary: After a claim, the text tells the reader how to receive it: "Let that sink in.", "Read that again.", "Sit with that.", "Think about that for a second." The command performs significance instead of showing it, and it presumes the claim was striking. It is a stock device of viral LinkedIn posts that generated posts reproduce.

positive: We cut the team in half and shipped twice as fast. Let that sink in.
Your customers don't care about your roadmap. Read that again.
Most burnout is a planning failure, not a character flaw. Sit with that.
Ninety percent of the budget went to meetings. Think about that for a second.
negative: Give the new process a week to sink in before you measure anything.
Read that chapter again before the exam on Friday.
Let the dough rest for an hour so the salt can sink in.
I had to read it twice because the contract language was so dense.

patterns.legitimate_use: A speaker or columnist may use the device once, deliberately, after a figure that is genuinely surprising and stated precisely. Instructions to reread a specific passage ("Read clause 4 again") are not emphasis commands and fall outside the detector.
patterns.fix: Delete the command. If the preceding claim needs weight, give it a number, a comparison or a consequence the reader can check.
patterns.prevention: Do not tell the reader to let something sink in, to read it again or to sit with it. Make the claim strong enough to stand alone.
patterns.notes: Mechanism: an imperative meta-comment on the reader's reaction, placed after a claim. Closest existing pattern: fragment-pathos (clipped closing fragments such as "That's it. That's the whole thing.") and payoff-announcement ("Here's the kicker:"). Payoff announcements come before the point; fragment pathos is a clipped statement about the content. The emphasis command follows the point, says nothing about the content and addresses the reader; it can occur in any position. The humanizer skill files "Let that sink in." under its dramatic one-line closers, so the boundary with fragment-pathos is close; the deterministic detector here matches only the reader-directed imperatives as whole sentences. "Full stop." from the LinkedIn analysis is left out because it is a fragment about the content (fragment-pathos territory).

patterns.name: Reasoning leak
patterns.summary: Traces of the writer's deliberation or task decomposition stay visible in the final text instead of leading straight to the result: "Let me think step by step", "Breaking this down:", "Here's my thought process", or narration of the writer's own moves and decisions ("I want to be exact about my own role here"). The reader gets the scaffolding along with the building.

negative: Let me know if the build fails again.

The committee approached the problem systematically and found three causes.

patterns.fix: Delete the planning phrase and the narration of your own moves. Start with the result, then give the reasons the reader needs.
patterns.prevention: Do not narrate your reasoning process or announce how you will approach the task ("Let me think step by step", "Breaking this down"). Deliver the result and the reasons directly.

patterns.name: Rhetorical self-answer
patterns.summary: A short rhetorical question that nobody asked, built from a bare noun phrase, is answered at once by a clipped, often fragmentary sentence ("The result? Devastating."). The question adds no information; it stages suspense for a point that a plain sentence would state faster.

positive: The result? Devastating.
The worst part? Nobody saw it coming.
The solution? It's simpler than you think.
We shipped on Friday. The scary part? This attack vector is perfect for developers.

patterns.fix: Delete the question and state the answer as a full sentence with its subject ("The result was a two-day outage"). If the suspense matters, earn it with the facts that lead up to the point.
patterns.prevention: Do not pose a short question and answer it yourself ("The result? Devastating."). State the point directly in a complete sentence.

patterns.name: Self-echo
patterns.summary: A distinctive word, phrase or image from earlier in the same text comes back as if it were a deliberate callback, while it is really the same narrow vocabulary recurring under topic pressure ("wearing the same italics ... wearing a different costume"). The repetition poses as a punchline and adds nothing.

detector.rubric: Find distinctive words, phrases or images (not ordinary function words or the topic's key terms) that appear two or more times in the text, where a later occurrence is staged as a callback or punchline (often at a paragraph or section end) but adds no new meaning to the first. Typical signs: the same unusual verb or metaphor reused for different things, a paragraph closing with a phrase lifted from the opening, a coined image recurring in each section. Do not count consistent technical terms, deliberate refrains in speeches, poems or songs, and callbacks that change or resolve the meaning of the first use. Return each echoed phrase as a hit with its occurrences.

positive: The old dashboard was wearing the same italics as the report it replaced. Six months later, the new one is the same problem wearing a different costume.

patterns.fix: Cut the echo, or replace it with a statement that says something new. Keep a callback only if the second use changes or resolves the first.
patterns.prevention: Do not reuse a distinctive phrase or image from earlier in the text as a closing punchline. Say something new or end the paragraph.

patterns.name: Source-availability hedge
patterns.summary: Instead of stating a fact, the text comments on the state of its sources: details "are limited in available sources" or "not widely documented", the content is offered "based on available information", a person "maintains a low profile", or a source "does not by itself establish" a claim. Search-enabled chatbots produce these remarks when their search returns little; the remark fills the place of the missing fact, and the claim about the sources is itself unverified.

positive: While specific details about the village's economy are limited, agriculture likely plays a central role.
Though her early recordings aren't widely documented, they highlight her versatility as a performer.
Below is a detailed overview based on available information:
The founder maintains a low profile, and little is said about his other business interests.
A listing in the heritage register does not by itself establish that the building is historically significant.
Information about the local fauna is sparse in the provided search results.
negative: The data that support the findings are available from the corresponding author on request.
The court found that the evidence does not establish that the defendant knew of the defect.
Little is known about the composer's early life because the parish records burned in 1870.
The search results page now loads in under 200 milliseconds.
The bug is well documented in the issue tracker, with steps to reproduce.

patterns.legitimate_use: Researchers, journalists and encyclopedists legitimately report gaps in the record when they name what they searched and why the gap matters ("the parish records burned in 1870"). Police and agency statements say "based on available information" as a standard caveat. Flag the remark when it stands in place of research, names no source, and is followed by generic or speculative filler.
patterns.fix: Find the missing fact in a named source, or cut the sentence. If a gap is relevant, state what was checked and what is missing ("No parish register survives for 1820 to 1850"), then move on without speculative filler.
patterns.prevention: Do not comment on how much information is available. State what a named source says, or leave the point out.
patterns.notes: Mechanism: the writer reports on its own search instead of on the subject, often as a preamble to speculation ("While specific details ... are limited, X likely ..."). Closest existing patterns: cya-disclaimer ("It's important to note that ...", a meta announcement of importance) and vague-attribution (claims backed by unnamed experts or studies). This pattern adds no authority and announces nothing important; it disclaims the evidence base. The Wikipedia guide dates the forms: "it's important to note" caveats in 2023 to 2024, "not widely documented" and "maintains a low profile" with web-search chatbots in 2024 to 2025, and "does not by itself establish" style epistemic caveats from mid-2026, which it says were nearly unheard of before. The detector leaves out "not publicly available" and the bare "does not establish that", which are standard in data-availability statements and legal writing. Single-source observation.

patterns.name: Stacked nouns
patterns.summary: Chains of three or more nouns in which the leading nouns modify the head noun pile up in English prose ("reader-patience budget", "model evaluation pipeline failure mode"). Each chain compresses a relation that a preposition or a verb would make explicit, and the reader has to reconstruct it.

detector.rubric: Find noun chains of three or more nouns (hyphenated or not) in which the leading nouns modify the last one, such as "reader-patience budget" or "deployment risk mitigation plan". Count a chain only if it is not an established term or name (customer service team, data center cooling system, United Nations Security Council, product names) and if unpacking it with a preposition or verb would make the relation clearer ("the patience readers have left"). Do not count adjective-noun phrases (see premodifier-stacking), German compound words, which are standard orthography, and technical identifiers. Return each chain as a hit.

positive: Every extra paragraph draws down the reader-patience budget.
The model evaluation pipeline failure mode went unnoticed for weeks.
We need a deployment risk mitigation plan before the release.
negative: The customer service team answers calls until 8 p.m.
The data center cooling system failed on Tuesday.
Readers lose patience with every extra paragraph.

patterns.legitimate_use: Technical and administrative English has many established noun compounds, and headlines compress by convention. Flag ad-hoc chains in running prose where a preposition or verb would make the relation explicit.
patterns.fix: Unpack the chain: put the head noun first and attach the modifiers with prepositions or a clause ("a plan to reduce the risks of deployment").
patterns.prevention: Avoid chains of three or more nouns that are not established terms. Use prepositions or a clause to show how the nouns relate.
patterns.notes: Independent sources: arxiv-2610-29162 (abstract and full text) and slhck-claudish. English only: German writes noun compounds as one word by rule, and unnatural compound chains in German are covered by german-stock-phrases. patterns.name: Synonym cycling

detector.rubric: Within each paragraph, find referents (a product, system, screen, group of people, organization or concept) that are named by three or more different noun phrases although one precise term would serve throughout, for example "dashboard", "interface", "portal" and "analytics hub" for the same screen. Do not flag deliberate distinctions (a broader term used once to widen a claim, terms the text defines as different things), quoted product names, or legal and technical texts that repeat one defined term. patterns.notes: Threshold set so that at most 4 % of the human reference corpus (pre-2022 texts, de and en) triggers it; separation from AI-generated text is not yet measured. Encyclopedic and web prose often contains several real three-item enumerations: with a fixed count of 3 triads per text 18 % (de) and 21 % (en) of the human texts triggered. Texts above short_text_max_words therefore use a density, 6.5 or more triads per 500 words (3 triads in a text of up to 230 words, 13 in 1,000 words); the densest human texts reach 12.5 to 14 per 500 words. A fixed count would have to be 7 per text to meet the limit, which misses short and medium texts and lets long ones accumulate freely. Short texts use a paragraph count instead (2 or more triads in one paragraph), because a single triad in a few dozen words would already exceed the density. A "from X to Y to Z" chain is a triad in the sense of this pattern, but the triad metric does not count it, so the host model should count it; false-range covers only two-endpoint ranges with closed vocabularies.

patterns.name: Unfilled template placeholder
patterns.summary: Slots of a fill-in template remain in the published text: bracketed labels or instructions ("[Your Name]", "[Company Name]", "[Insert statistic here]"), capitalised URL tokens ("INSERT_SOURCE_URL"), parenthetical instructions ("(Add your channel URL here)") or placeholder dates ("2026-xx-xx"). Chat assistants produce such templates when details are missing, sometimes even when told not to; a slot left in the text shows that nobody completed or read the draft.

patterns.legitimate_use: Templates that are meant to be filled in (a form-letter library, a mail-merge source, a style guide that shows the slots, documentation that tells readers to replace a value) contain placeholders on purpose. patterns.fix: Fill every slot with the real value or delete the sentence that depends on it. If the value is unknown, find it before publishing; never publish a sentence built around a missing fact.
patterns.prevention: Do not output bracketed slots or placeholder values in a deliverable. Ask for the missing detail or write the sentence so that it does not need it.
patterns.notes: Mechanism: the generated text is a template, and the writer published it without completing it. No existing pattern covers it; the closest are assistant-self-reference and format-bleed, which are also copy-and-paste residue but concern the assistant's voice and unrendered markup. The bracket rule is case-sensitive and limited to slot words that open a placeholder ("Your", "Insert", "Company", "Recipient" and similar) and excludes markdown links "[text](url)", so editorial brackets in quotations do not match. Upper-case tokens are limited to INSERT_ and PASTE_ because documentation legitimately uses YOUR_API_KEY-style variables. patterns.legitimate_use: Some genres keep sentence length steady on purpose: step-by-step instructions, legal clauses, glossary entries, verse with a fixed meter. Lists and tables are units of their own and do not count as paragraphs. Treat the finding as a revision hint for running prose.

patterns.prevention: Vary sentence length within and across paragraphs. Mix short sentences with longer ones and do not give every paragraph the same number of sentences.

sources.note: Coefficient of variation of sentence length below 0.4 counts as monotone; human texts typically range from 0.6 to 1.2. Measured over a whole text, so it is a different quantification from the paragraph runs used here.

patterns.notes: Threshold set so that at most 4 % of the human reference corpus (pre-2022 texts, de and en) triggers it; separation from AI-generated text is not yet measured. The metric is the coefficient of variation (CV) of sentence length pooled over a run of consecutive paragraphs; a CV of 0.38 corresponds to a standard deviation of about 6 to 7 words at 17 words per sentence. Paragraphs with fewer than three sentences break a run. Without that rule, runs of one-line paragraphs on web pages (menu labels, product features, hard-wrapped lines) made up the human triggers, and runs of four paragraphs needed a CV below 0.1 to stay within the limit. With at least three sentences per paragraph, runs of four paragraphs and a CV below 0.38, 3.5 % (de) and 2.3 % (en) of the 520 human texts trigger; 11.5 % (de) and 7.3 % (en) contain such a run at all. The remaining human triggers are running prose (encyclopedia articles, reviews, news digests). Shorter runs or shorter paragraphs need a stricter limit at the same rate: runs of three paragraphs allow a CV below 0.31 with at least three sentences and below 0.26 with at least two. The constant number of sentences per paragraph is left to the host model.

patterns.name: Ambient glow and glass decoration
patterns.summary: Surfaces are dressed with atmosphere that carries no content: blurred colored orbs or aurora/mesh blobs behind the hero, a radial color halo or spotlight, zero-offset colored glow shadows on cards and buttons, frosted-glass panels (backdrop blur over translucent white or black), and faint grid or dot overlays. Three independent design skills implement checks for these as generated-UI signatures and practitioners list glowing heroes and blobs among the tells; a Reddit-mining study found blob and glass complaints rare, so the pattern is judged on visible density, not on any single effect.

detector.rubric: Look at backgrounds and surfaces, mainly the hero and the cards. Count these decoration types: (a) blurred colored orbs, blobs, aurora or mesh gradients floating behind content; (b) a saturated radial halo or spotlight glow behind a headline, product shot or section; (c) colored glow shadows around cards, buttons or text (light spreading evenly on all sides, often on a dark page); (d) frosted-glass panels, translucent white or black with a blur of what lies behind, used on cards or sections rather than only on a sticky navigation or overlay; (e) a faint square grid or dot-matrix pattern laid over the background for texture. Flag the page when two or more types appear, or when one type repeats on most sections or cards. Count one hit per page. When only the source is available, signs are blur-3xl or filter: blur() on absolutely positioned colored divs, radial-gradient(... transparent) backgrounds, box-shadow with 0 0 offsets and a colored rgba value, backdrop-blur or backdrop-filter: blur() with bg-white/10 or rgba(255,255,255,0.1), and background-image built from repeating linear-gradient lines or radial-gradient dots at a fixed pixel size. Does not count: one blurred sticky header or a modal backdrop; real photography of light, sky or space; a texture that belongs to the subject (a blueprint grid on an architecture page, graph paper on a math tool, a map); a canvas or editor whose grid is functional; a single restrained glow on one focal element in a design that is otherwise flat. Describe the visible pattern only; do not infer how the page was made.

positive: Dark hero for a project-management app with two large blurred purple and cyan orbs behind the headline, a faint square grid over the whole background, and feature cards glowing with a soft violet halo.
Light landing page where every card is a frosted translucent white panel with a blur of pastel blobs behind it, and the signup button has a colored glow on all sides.
Hero section with a bright radial spotlight of teal light behind the headline fading into black, and a dot-matrix pattern covering the rest of the page.
negative: A sticky navigation bar with a light backdrop blur over the scrolling content; all other surfaces are solid.
Page for an observatory whose hero is a real long-exposure photograph of the night sky.
Architecture studio site using a blueprint grid as the background of its project drawings section, matching its plan drawings.

patterns.legitimate_use: Atmospheric or immersive briefs (music, events, games, night-time venues) where light is the concept, a brand that owns a glow or glass look, operating-system style materials used for overlays and navigation, and functional grids on canvas, map or measurement surfaces. The pattern is stacking these effects as default decoration.
patterns.fix: Remove the orbs, halos, glow shadows and background overlays; give surfaces a solid or subtly tinted background. Express elevation with lightness steps or a neutral shadow with offset and blur, and keep blur only where content scrolls under an overlay. If the page needs a visual, show the product, the place or the people instead.
patterns.prevention: Build surfaces from solid fills, tinted wells, hairlines and neutral offset shadows. Let the hero carry something specific to the subject: the product in use, a photograph, a diagram, a real texture from the subject's world. Use at most one atmospheric effect, and only when the brief is about light or mood; never add blurred orbs, aurora blobs, colored glow shadows, glass cards or grid and dot overlays as filler.

patterns.name: Card-chopped uniform page
patterns.summary: Nearly every piece of content sits in its own rounded box with the same radius, padding and shadow, stacked in full-width sections of identical vertical padding inside one centered max-width column, so the page reads as an inventory of evenly weighted tiles (a "dashboard") instead of an argument with emphasis. Nothing breaks the column, overlaps, bleeds or changes rhythm. Anthropic's design skill lists "the SaaS-card kit: content chopped into identical rounded cards, one border-radius on everything regardless of hierarchy" among the traits generated design clusters around, a community catalog describes marketing pages "chopped into evenly weighted rounded rectangles", and a developer reports generated layouts are "almost always vertically stacked, full-width sections with centered content".

detector.rubric: Judge the full-page screenshot. Flag the page (one hit) when all three hold: (1) in at least three different sections the content (features, steps, quotes, stats, prices, FAQ items, plain text paragraphs) is placed in boxed cards, i.e. rounded rectangles with their own background, border or shadow, and the cards share one radius and one shadow regardless of their importance; boxes nested inside boxes count extra; (2) all sections use the same centered content column and similar vertical padding, so the section edges line up like a stack of equal slabs; (3) no section uses an asymmetric, full-bleed, overlapping or editorial layout (text running beside a large image, a wide quotation, a long reading column, an image breaking the grid). In the HTML/CSS source: the same card class string repeated across sections (rounded-xl/2xl border bg-card shadow-sm/lg p-6), every section wrapped in the same container (mx-auto max-w-6xl/7xl px-4 py-16/24), shadcn/ui <Card> components used for text that is not an item in a collection. Does not count: dashboards, admin panels and app screens, where cards are the right container for independent widgets; e-commerce listings and galleries; a page that boxes only one or two genuinely distinct elements (a pricing table, a sign-up form) and otherwise uses open layout; documentation with callout boxes. Describe the visible pattern only; do not infer how the page was made.

positive: Landing page of a law firm where the hero subtext, the three practice areas, the 'About us' paragraph, each testimonial, each FAQ answer and the contact details all sit in white rounded cards with the same soft shadow, every section 96px tall in padding and centered in the same 1200px column.

Marketing page for a podcast chopped into a mosaic of evenly weighted rounded tiles, each with a micro-icon, a short label and one number or sentence, so the episode list, host bio and subscribe links look like dashboard widgets.

Page of a recipe newsletter where the single explanatory paragraph is itself wrapped in a bordered card, inside a larger tinted card, inside a centered section, and every following section repeats the same boxed structure.
negative: Analytics dashboard with cards for independent charts and KPIs.
Editorial page with a full-bleed photograph, a long left-aligned reading column, a pull quote spanning the margin and only the newsletter sign-up form in a box.
Online shop category page with a grid of product cards.

patterns.legitimate_use: Applications and dashboards, collections of genuinely independent items, and brands whose identity is a deliberate modular grid with varied tile sizes and real content in each tile.
patterns.fix: Remove boxes from content that is not an item in a collection and let typography, spacing and alignment group it instead; never nest cards. Vary section width and rhythm: let one section run full-bleed, set a long text in a reading column, put an image beside the text, and give the most important section more space than the rest.
patterns.prevention: Use a card only for an item that is one of a set and can be acted on separately. Group everything else with spacing, rules, alignment and type scale. Plan the page as a sequence with emphasis: decide which section is the climax and give it a different width, layout or scale; mix at least two layout modes (for example a reading column, a split section and a full-bleed image) and vary vertical spacing with the content. An explicit brand or user wish overrides this.

sources.note: 'the SaaS-card kit: content chopped into identical rounded cards, one border-radius on everything regardless of hierarchy, the same soft grey shadow (rgba(0,0,0,.1)) under each'; called a default rather than a choice.

'Even simple marketing pages get chopped into evenly weighted rounded rectangles with eyebrow labels, micro-icons, and one stat per tile'; result is 'everything, equally'; bento is fine 'when the content actually wants modular chunks'.
'AI-generated layouts are almost always vertically stacked, full-width sections with centered content'; 'Every AI-generated component has `rounded-2xl shadow-lg p-6` somewhere'.
'Cards nested in cards'; 'Cards are the lazy container; nested cards are always wrong' (derived from Anthropic's skill).

patterns.notes: Merges the proposed "bento grid as default feature showcase" and "card-everything" candidates: the readable sources on bento (aismells, the YC design review) describe evenly weighted tiles, not a mosaic of deliberately uneven tiles, and one source recommends a bento with a genuinely larger cell as a fix. Radius, shadow color and glass effects as such belong to visual-style patterns; this pattern judges only the boxing and the uniform page structure.

patterns.name: Accessibility gaps of the default look
patterns.summary: The default styling and markup leave the same accessibility holes: light-gray body or helper text on white below 4.5:1, images without alt or with filler alt ("image", "hero image"), icon-only buttons and links without an accessible name, generic names ("Submit", "Click here", "Learn more"), placeholder text in place of form labels, and focus outlines removed (outline-none, focus:outline-none) without a visible replacement. Studies of generated pages report low contrast, unlabeled inputs and missing focus handling in GPT-4o output, focus indicators on 56% of elements under a plain prompt, and generic buttons, vague links and poor alt text as the top semantic violations in 300 generated UIs. The same defects are very common on human-made pages, so the pattern only counts together with other findings.

detector.rubric: Read the HTML/JSX/CSS. Check five defect types, one hit per type found on the page: (1) Contrast: body, helper or footer text styled with light grays on white or near-white (text-gray-400/text-gray-300/text-slate-400 on bg-white or bg-gray-50, #999 or lighter on #fff), or white text on a light gradient; judge from the class or computed colors, roughly below 4.5:1 for normal text. (2) Images: meaningful img elements (product shots, team photos, diagrams) with missing alt or filler alt (alt="image", alt="hero", alt="placeholder", the file name). (3) Names: icon-only buttons or links (svg or icon font only, e.g. hamburger, close, social icons, carousel arrows) without aria-label, title or visually hidden text; or several links and buttons whose only text is "Learn more", "Read more", "Click here", "Submit". (4) Labels: inputs whose only label is the placeholder (no label element, no aria-label or aria-labelledby). (5) Focus: outline-none, focus:outline-none, outline: 0 or :focus {outline: none} on interactive elements without a focus-visible ring or other visible replacement. Trigger at two or more defect types, and only when at least two other web patterns from this catalog triggered on the same page (web patterns carry no weight, so this co-occurrence is part of the rubric, not of a scored dependency). Does not count: gray text that meets 4.5:1 (e.g. text-gray-600 or darker on white) or large display text that meets 3:1; decorative images with alt="" or aria-hidden; icon buttons with an aria-label or sr-only text; a "Learn more" link with aria-label or aria-describedby giving its target; outline removed but replaced with focus-visible:ring or a box-shadow focus style; floating labels implemented with a real label element. If only the rendered page is available, judge contrast and missing focus rings by tabbing through the page; leave the other checks to the source. Describe the visible pattern only; do not infer how the page was made.

positive:
Trusted by teams worldwide

on bg-white, with no aria-label, and with no label.
Every feature card ends in Learn more with no other context, team photos use alt="image", and the global CSS contains *:focus { outline: none; }.
Footer row of social icons without accessible names, and footer text in text-slate-400 on bg-slate-50.
negative:
...

on white (about 7:1), decorative blob , and a menu button with Open menu.
<input class="outline-none focus-visible:ring-2 focus-visible:ring-offset-2" id="email"> with <label for="email">Work email</label>.
Three 'Read more' links each with aria-label="Read more about pricing" etc., and a single light-gray caption under a chart that is set in large bold type meeting 3:1.

patterns.legitimate_use: None of these defects is a deliberate design choice; low-contrast text can be acceptable only for disabled controls and purely decorative text. The reason for the threshold and the co-occurrence condition in the rubric is that these gaps are widespread on human-made pages too (WebAIM: low-contrast text on 83.9% of top home pages), so alone they indicate an inaccessible page, not a generic default look.
patterns.fix: Darken body and helper text to at least 4.5:1, write alt text that says what each meaningful image shows (alt="" for decoration), give every icon-only control an aria-label or visually hidden text, rewrite generic link and button text to name the destination or action, add real label elements, and replace removed outlines with a visible focus-visible style. Verify with an automated checker and a keyboard pass.
patterns.prevention: Treat accessibility as part of the default style, not an optional pass: pick text colors from tokens that meet 4.5:1 on their background, never remove focus outlines without a visible focus-visible replacement, give every control a visible label or an accessible name that states its action or destination ("Download the report", not "Click here"), and write real alt text. A brand palette that fails contrast must be adjusted for text, not used as is.

sources.note: 541 semantic violations in 300 generated UIs: generic button labels 27%, vague link text 26% ('Read more', 'Learn more'), poor alt text 20% (alt='image'), ARIA 14%, generic form labels 12%; strong model differences.

GPT-4o page without accessibility instructions: low contrast on headings, buttons, footer links and hover text (1.71-2.23:1), inputs without labels (placeholders), placeholder or empty alt, not keyboard navigable, modal focus not managed.
Plain prompt: focus indicators on 56% of elements (98% with an accessibility prompt), keyboard access 48%; control UIs 'often relied on browser defaults or omitted focus indicators entirely'.
GPT-4 form components: required field without a visible label (placeholder only), color-only error states, ARIA added without need.
One vibe-coded site: over fifty low-contrast instances (2.77:1, 1.7:1) and twelve label problems.
'light gray text on white backgrounds is a very common AI-generated default'; no visible focus states; missing alt text.
Agent-facing: visible focus ring on every focusable element, icon-only buttons named, every control labelled.
Counter-evidence: naive GPT-4o and Qwen2.5-Coder output had fewer contrast and alt-text violations than human code; Qwen showed FocusRemoveFail issues.

patterns.name: Default sans as the only typeface
patterns.summary: The whole page, display headings included, is set in one stock sans-serif (Inter, Roboto, Open Sans, Lato, Arial or the system UI font), and hierarchy comes only from size and weight steps, often shallow ones. Anthropic and OpenAI both tell their models to avoid exactly these default stacks, independent design skills list them as the faces "every model reaches for first", and an HCI preprint describes the homogenized vibe-coded site as using "standard sans-serif typography".

detector.rubric: Look at the headline, section headings, body text, buttons and navigation. Flag the page when all of them use a single neutral grotesque sans of the Inter, Roboto, Open Sans, Lato, Arial, Helvetica or system-UI kind (even, closed shapes, no distinctive letterforms), with no second face for display or accents, and the type hierarchy is made only of bolder and larger versions of the same face. A flat scale (headings barely larger than body text) strengthens the hit. Count one hit per page. When only the source is available, signs are font-family: Inter, Roboto, 'Open Sans', Lato, Arial, system-ui, -apple-system or ui-sans-serif as the only family, Tailwind font-sans without a configured custom family, or one Google Fonts import of Inter. Does not count: a product UI, dashboard or documentation site where a neutral sans is the right working face; a page using the brand's own licensed typeface even if it is a sans; a page that pairs a neutral sans for body text with a distinct display or serif face; a high-contrast serif or italic serif headline (see stock-tasteful-palette). Describe the visible pattern only; do not infer how the page was made.

positive: Landing page for a wine shop where the hero headline, the navigation, the product cards and the footer are all set in the same neutral grotesque sans; the headline is just the body face at 56px bold.
Portfolio page for an illustrator set entirely in a system-UI sans, headings in semibold only slightly larger than the paragraphs.
Event page whose title, schedule and buttons all use one Inter-like sans in three weights, with no other face anywhere.
negative: Admin dashboard for a logistics team set in a neutral sans with tabular figures, where legibility at small sizes is the point.
Landing page that uses a condensed display face for headlines and a neutral sans for body text.
Company site in the brand's own commissioned sans-serif, which also appears on its packaging and signage.

patterns.legitimate_use: Interfaces, dashboards, documentation and forms where a neutral working face serves reading; a brand whose typeface is a neutral sans; a deliberate Swiss-style design that builds hierarchy through scale contrast, grid and spacing rather than a second face.
patterns.fix: Choose a display face that fits the subject and the brand and pair it with a readable body face; set a type scale with clear steps (at least a 1.25 ratio between levels) and keep weights to two or three. Keep the neutral sans only for interface text where it serves.
patterns.prevention: Decide typography before layout: pick a display face for its character in the subject's world (a grotesque from rail signage, a slab from old packaging, a humanist serif from print), a body face that reads well with it, and a scale with clear steps. Do not default to Inter, Roboto, Open Sans, Lato, Arial or system fonts, and do not swap to the next most common face (Space Grotesk, Geist) by reflex; use them only when the brand, the existing codebase or the brief names them.
