patterns.name: Emoji or stock line icons as feature marks
patterns.summary: Features, headings and list items are marked with emoji standing in for icons, or with icons from one stock line set (Lucide, Heroicons and similar) placed in small tinted rounded squares or circles, where the icons add no information the text does not already give. Three independent design skills ban emoji as icons and flag the icon-in-a-tinted-tile, an operator blog names "Lucide React icons (always)", and OpenAI's guide lists ornamental icons and icon rows as failures.

detector.rubric: Look at icons next to features, benefits, headings, list items and steps. Flag the page when (a) emoji (rocket, sparkles, lightning, check mark, fire and similar) serve as feature or heading icons, or (b) most such items carry a generic outline icon of uniform stroke from one stock set, set inside a small tinted square or circle in the accent color, and the icons are generic metaphors (lightning for speed, shield for security, sparkles for AI) rather than depictions of the product. Count one hit per page. When only the source is available, signs are imports from lucide-react, @heroicons/react or react-icons used for feature lists, wrappers like 'rounded-lg bg-indigo-100 p-3' or 'rounded-full bg-primary/10' around a single icon, or emoji characters inside headings and list items. Does not count: icons in navigation, toolbars, forms and controls where they label actions; a custom-drawn icon set made for the brand; product screenshots or illustrations; a single emoji in informal copy (covered by text patterns); status icons that carry meaning (error, success). Describe the visible pattern only; do not infer how the page was made.

positive: Feature list of a payroll tool where each item starts with an emoji: a rocket for 'Fast setup', a lock for 'Secure', sparkles for 'AI-powered'.
Benefits section where each benefit has a thin-outline lightning, shield or chart icon inside a pale violet rounded square, all icons from the same stroke set.

negative: Application toolbar with outline icons for bold, italic, link and undo, each with a tooltip.

patterns.legitimate_use: Icons that label controls and navigation; a consistent library icon set used functionally in an application; a custom icon family drawn for the brand; emoji in a deliberately playful or chat-based brand voice where the brief asks for them.
patterns.fix: Remove emoji used as icons. Replace generic icon tiles with something specific: a screenshot or crop of the feature, a small diagram, a number or fact, or plain typography. Where icons stay, set them inline with the text in the text color, without tinted tiles.
patterns.prevention: Mark features with evidence from the product or subject (a screenshot crop, a real photo, a concrete figure) or with typography alone. Use icons only where they help scanning or label an action, from one set used consistently, inline and in the text color. Do not use emoji as icons and do not put stock line icons in tinted squares or circles as decoration.

patterns.name: Generic imagery in place of the subject
patterns.summary: The hero and section images do not show the page's actual product, place, work or people but a stand-in that fits any business: a diverse team smiling at a laptop, abstract 3D blobs, flat or isometric vector scenes, or a dashboard mockup with filler charts. The image slot is filled by category instead of by subject. Practitioner critiques of AI-built sites name "the same smiling stock photos", stock photos "with no connection to your industry or location", 3D blobs and missing real product screenshots; design reviewers of vibe-coded sites said "every fake dashboard looks basically like" the same, and a design skill for coding agents shows flat vector illustrations as an agent's default.

detector.rubric: First state what the page is about from its headline and copy: a product (what it does), a place, a service, specific people. Then look at the hero image and the main section images. Flag the page when the hero image, or most of the section images, show a stand-in instead of that subject: (1) generic stock-type people scenes with no identifying link to this business (a diverse team smiling at a laptop in a bright office, a handshake, a headset agent, a person pointing at a screen); (2) abstract 3D renders used as the main visual (glossy blobs, spheres, rings, floating cubes, gradient glass shapes) on a page whose subject is not 3D art; (3) flat or isometric vector illustrations of generic people, servers, charts or devices that would fit any company; (4) a dashboard or app mockup with filler content: arbitrary line and bar charts, colored KPI tiles ("Revenue +12.5%", "Users 2,847"), sparklines or gray skeleton rectangles that do not match what the copy says the product does; (5) placeholder image boxes or broken image icons. Count one hit per page. From source only: image URLs from stock libraries or placeholder services with alt texts like "team collaborating"; a hero "screenshot" built in JSX from hard-coded random number arrays and generic labels; illustration files named like hero-illustration.svg from an illustration kit. Does not count: real screenshots of the product showing features the copy describes (even framed or stylized); photos of the actual place, team, products or work, recognizable by specific details (signage, the dishes, the building, the workshop); custom illustrations that explain this product's specific mechanism; abstract or 3D visuals on pages for 3D, art or design studios showing their own work; a clearly labelled demo dashboard whose metrics match the product's domain; CSS background glows and gradients behind content (a decorative-effect pattern, not an image choice). Describe the visible pattern only; do not infer how the page was made.

positive: Hero of an accounting firm in a small town: a wide photo of five young professionals of different ethnicities laughing around a laptop in a glass-walled office; nothing on the page shows the firm's office, staff or town.

patterns.name: Gradient-filled headline text
patterns.summary: Headlines, key words or big numbers are filled with a color gradient (background-clip: text) as the default way to add emphasis, instead of weight, size, a typeface or one solid accent color. Three independent design skills name gradient text, especially on headings and metrics, as a generated-page tell, and a developer write-up lists "hero section with gradient text" in the default look.

detector.rubric: Look at the hero headline, section headings and large figures. Flag the page when at least one heading, a word inside a heading or a display-size number is filled with a multi-hue color gradient (the letters change color along their length, e.g. from violet to blue or from pink to orange) on an otherwise solid-colored page. Count one hit per page, however many headings carry it. When only the source is available, signs are bg-clip-text together with text-transparent and bg-gradient-to-* or bg-linear-to-* utilities, or CSS background-clip: text / -webkit-background-clip: text with -webkit-text-fill-color: transparent over a linear-gradient. Does not count: a logo or wordmark that is itself drawn with a gradient as part of the brand identity; text over a photo or texture (image fill) that is a deliberate typographic illustration; a single-hue tone ramp barely visible as a gradient; solid colored words used for emphasis (judge those under other patterns). Describe the visible pattern only; do not infer how the page was made.

positive: Hero headline 'Ship your ideas faster' in black, with the words 'faster' filled by a violet-to-blue gradient.
Pricing section where each plan price ('$29', '$79') is set in a large pink-to-orange gradient fill on white cards.
Every section heading on a dark page is filled with a cyan-to-purple gradient, while body text is grey.
negative: The company's registered wordmark in the navigation uses a two-color gradient that also appears on its app icon.
A poster-style headline filled with a photograph of ocean water, used as the page's single typographic illustration.
A headline in solid dark green with one word in bold.

patterns.legitimate_use: A brand wordmark drawn with a gradient, an editorial or event page where a gradient letterform is the one deliberate typographic idea, or a brief that asks for it. The pattern is gradient fill as the routine emphasis device.
patterns.fix: Set headings and figures in one solid ink. Carry emphasis with weight, size, a display face or a single solid accent color; if a gradient is wanted, move it to one non-text element.
patterns.prevention: Give headlines one solid color and create hierarchy with a deliberate display typeface, size steps and weight. When a word needs emphasis, rewrite the headline or use weight; reserve the accent color for actions. Use gradient-filled text only when the brand mark or the brief calls for it.

patterns.name: Identical icon feature-card grid
patterns.summary: Features or benefits are shown as a row or grid of three, four or six same-size cards, each an icon on top, a two- or three-word title and one line of description, with no card larger, no image of the actual thing, and no difference in rhythm. Equal cells make every item look equally important and say nothing a list could not. A corpus scan of Show HN landing pages checked for "Identical feature cards, each with an icon on top", design reviewers of vibe-coded sites called the icon-on-top 3x2 tile grid "quite common" and "very non-original", and several practitioner write-ups name the three-card row as the stock feature section.

detector.rubric: Find sections laid out as a grid or row of 3 to 8 sibling tiles. Flag a section when the tiles have the same size and the same internal structure, and each consists mainly of a small icon (often in a tinted rounded square or circle) above or beside a short title and a one- or two-line description, with no product image, data, link destination or detail that distinguishes one tile from another. Equal-size tiles labeled as a "bento" grid count when they follow the same icon-title-line recipe. Count one hit per section; flag the page at one hit. In the HTML/CSS source: a container with grid-cols-3 / md:grid-cols-3 / lg:grid-cols-4 / grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr) whose children are rendered from one array map with the fields icon, title, description, each child an identical card component (often with lucide or heroicons icons). Does not count: a grid of real items that are naturally equivalent (team members with photos, products with images and prices, blog posts with thumbnails, integrations with real logos); a feature section where tiles differ in size and content because one feature matters more and shows a real screenshot; a comparison table; a short three-item icon row used as a compact summary under a section that already explains the features in depth. Describe the visible pattern only; do not infer how the page was made.

positive: Section 'Why choose us' with three equal white cards in a row; each has a purple icon in a rounded square (lightning bolt, shield, clock), the titles 'Lightning fast', 'Secure by default', 'Save time' and one gray sentence each.
A 3x2 grid of six identical dark tiles, each an outline icon on top, a bold two-word heading and one line of text, on the page of a yoga studio, with no photograph of the studio or the classes.

Four equal cards across the width ('Easy setup', 'Analytics', 'Integrations', 'Support'), each with a centered icon, title and one-line description, repeated with the same layout in a second section further down.
negative: Grid of six product cards, each with a different product photograph, name, price and 'Add to cart' button.
Team section with four equal cards showing real portrait photographs, names and roles.
Feature section alternating full-width rows, each with a large real screenshot on one side and two paragraphs on the other.

patterns.legitimate_use: Truly parallel items of equal weight, each backed by real content (product listings, people, locations, plan features), and compact icon rows that summarize detail given elsewhere.
patterns.fix: Rank the features and show the one that matters most with a real screenshot, photograph or demo at a larger size; merge or cut the minor ones; replace generic icons with the actual interface or object; vary tile sizes and section rhythm to express the ranking, or turn the items into connected prose or a plain list.
patterns.prevention: Do not present features as identical icon-title-sentence cards. Decide which two or three features matter most, show each with real evidence (a screenshot, a photograph, numbers from the product, a short example) and give the most important one more space. Use a grid of equal cells only for items that really are equal and each have their own image or data. An explicit brand or user wish overrides this.

patterns.name: Invented testimonials
patterns.summary: The testimonial slot of a page template is filled with quotes nobody can trace: placeholder-sounding names, a job title with no company or with a fictional one, an initials circle or generic headshot, five stars on every card and praise that would fit any product. Practitioner checklists for sites built with AI tools and site builders name testimonials and star ratings "nobody gave the AI" and "testimonials from people who do not exist" as a typical pre-launch defect, and a developer essay describes templates and AI builders inserting "three generic avatars" with randomly generated quotes.

detector.rubric: Find the testimonial, review or "what our customers say" section (cards, carousel, quote block). Flag it when the quotes carry no verifiable attribution and show at least two of these signs: (1) names that read as placeholders or stock pairs ("Jane Doe", "John D.", "Sarah Johnson", first name plus initial); (2) a job title with no company ("Marketing Lead", "VP of Growth"), a vague company ("a Fortune 500 company", "TechCorp", "Acme Inc.") or an invented-sounding company nobody could look up; (3) avatars that are initials in colored circles, generic studio headshots, or no image; (4) a uniform five-star row on every card; (5) quotes that praise generic qualities (time saved, "game-changer", productivity, support) with no detail of this product, its features, a number or a situation; (6) the same quote, name or face repeated in the row, or all quotes of near-identical length and rhythm. Count one hit per page. From source only: a hard-coded testimonials array whose entries all have rating 5, avatar URLs from placeholder-avatar or random-face services, or initials computed from the name. Does not count: testimonials with full name, a real-looking organization and product-specific detail; embedded third-party review widgets that show the platform, date and mixed ratings; video testimonials; a theme or template demo page that sells the template and labels its content as sample; testimonials explicitly anonymized for a stated reason (health, legal) that still describe a specific case; a single pull quote from a named press article with a link. Describe the visible pattern only; do not infer how the page was made.

positive: Three white cards under 'Loved by thousands': each has five yellow stars, a 40-word quote ('This tool completely transformed how our team works. We save hours every week!'), a colored circle with initials 'SJ', 'MC', 'ER', and the lines 'Sarah Johnson, Product Manager', 'Michael Chen, CTO', 'Emily Rodriguez, Marketing Director' with no company names.

Carousel of testimonials on a local bakery's site: 'Absolutely the best experience ever! Highly recommend!', signed 'Jessica M., Happy Customer', with a generic smiling studio headshot; the next slide uses the same headshot with another name.

Testimonial grid on a developer tool page: six quotes of identical length about 'seamless integration' and 'incredible support', attributed to 'Alex Rivera, Senior Engineer at TechFlow' and 'Priya Patel, Founder of Nexus Labs', each with five stars.
negative: A single testimonial with a named person, their role at a named regional hospital, a photo taken on site and a quote that describes how the scheduling feature replaced a paper rota on night shifts.
An embedded review-platform widget showing 4.6 average from 212 reviews, with dates, a few three-star reviews and links to the platform.
A template marketplace preview page with obviously fictional testimonials, under a banner saying 'Demo content: replace with your own'.

patterns.legitimate_use: Real, consented testimonials, even short ones; a template or theme demo that labels its sample content; illustrative user stories clearly marked as illustrative personas rather than customers.
patterns.fix: Delete every quote that cannot be traced to a real customer who agreed to be quoted. Replace the section with one or two real testimonials (full name, organization where allowed, a concrete situation or result), a link to an independent review platform, or remove the section until real quotes exist. Drop the uniform five-star rows unless the rating comes from a named source.
patterns.prevention: Do not write testimonials. If the brief provides real quotes, set them with the person's real name, role and organization and keep their wording; let them be uneven in length. If it provides none, leave the section out or put in a clearly labelled slot for the owner ("Add a real customer quote here") and list it as an open item; show the product working instead (a screenshot, a demo, a worked example). Never invent names, faces, companies or star ratings.

patterns.name: Non-functional controls presented as working
patterns.summary: The page shows controls that look finished but do nothing: navigation, footer and "Sign in" links pointing to "#", buttons without a handler, newsletter and contact forms with no action and no submit logic (or a handler that only prevents the default and logs), a search field that searches nothing, data that is hardcoded or kept in component state and gone on reload. The interface promises features the page does not have. Practitioner checklists for vibe-coded sites name buttons with "no onClick handler wired up, or link to #" and forms that show no success or error state; an agency reports forms that "look fine but often fail to actually submit & store data"; a studio describes generated interfaces whose "buttons are there" while "the data behind them is hardcoded".

detector.rubric: Read the HTML/JSX and the scripts. List the controls a visitor would expect to work: primary and footer navigation links, sign-in/sign-up/get-started buttons, forms (newsletter, contact, waitlist, login), search fields, social links, "Download"/"Book a demo" buttons. Mark a control dead when: an a element has href="#", href="" or javascript:void(0) and no click handler and is not an in-page anchor; a button has no onClick/handler, no type="submit" inside a working form and no listener attached in the scripts; a form has no action (or action="#") and its submit handler is missing, only calls preventDefault, only logs, only shows an alert or toast without sending anything, or sets local state; a search input has no form, handler or results logic. Count one hit per page when at least two different dead controls are presented as working features (no "coming soon", disabled state or demo label). Does not count: in-page anchors (href="#pricing") that match an existing id; href="#" with a real handler attached by addEventListener or a framework router; forms handled by a named service (Netlify data-netlify, Formspree, a server action, fetch() to an API route); controls that are visibly disabled or labelled "coming soon"; files clearly presented as a mockup, template or component demo; a single forgotten link in an otherwise working page. If only the rendered page is available, count controls that visibly lead nowhere (URL ends in #, no navigation, no feedback after submit). Describe the visible pattern only; do not infer how the page was made.

patterns.name: Non-semantic page structure (div soup)
patterns.summary: The page is built from generic div and span elements styled to look structured: no header, nav, main or footer landmarks, headings picked for their size rather than the outline (no h1, several h1, skipped levels, or styled divs and paragraphs as headings), and clickable divs or spans in place of buttons and links. The visual hierarchy exists only in CSS, so assistive technology, search engines and keyboard users get a flat page. Studies of LLM-generated pages report divs used "exclusively" with landmark coverage of 11% and correct heading hierarchy of 33% under a plain prompt, a missing main landmark and missing h1, and missing main elements and content outside landmarks among the most frequent violations; practitioner checklists name clickable divs and several h1 per page.

detector.rubric: Read the HTML/JSX of the whole page. Check three things. (1) Landmarks: is there a main element (or role="main") and are the site header, primary navigation and footer marked as header, nav and footer (or the matching roles)? (2) Heading outline: list h1-h6 in document order; flag no h1, more than one h1 on a single-page layout, a jump of more than one level downward (h1 to h3, h2 to h4), or visible section titles that are div, p or span elements with heading-size classes (text-3xl font-bold, font-size 2rem) instead of h2/h3. (3) Interactive elements: div or span with onClick, @click or addEventListener('click') that acts as a button or link, without a native element; role="button" plus tabindex plus a key handler mitigates but still counts as a weak sign. Count one hit per page when at least two of the three checks fail, or when check 3 fails for a primary control (main CTA, menu toggle, form submit). Does not count: pages that use landmarks and a correct outline but also many layout divs (divs are fine for layout); component files that are clearly fragments rendered inside a layout which supplies the landmarks; a second h1 inside a modal or a separate article element where the outline is still coherent; a heading level skipped once in a footer; custom widgets that correctly use role, tabindex and keyboard handling (e.g. a listbox); a single-purpose app screen whose one heading is h1. patterns.name: Numbered how-it-works steps
patterns.summary: A "How it works" section shows three (sometimes four) equal columns or cards marked with large numerals or numbered circles (1, 2, 3 or 01, 02, 03), each with a short title and one line, often joined by a thin connector line. The numbering is applied whether or not the content is a real sequence, and the three steps are usually generic ("Sign up", "Connect", "Grow"). A corpus scan of Show HN landing pages scored "Numbered '1, 2, 3' step sequences" as a layout pattern, and Anthropic's design skill notes that "Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03)" where the content is not a sequence.

detector.rubric: Flag a section (one hit per page) that consists of three to five equal columns, cards or rows each led by a prominent ordinal marker (a large digit, "01"-style numeral, "Step 1" label or a digit in a circle or badge) followed by a short title and one or two lines of text, when at least one of these holds: the items are not an actual ordered process (they could be read in any order: "Fast", "Secure", "Scalable" numbered 01-03); the steps are generic and could belong to any product ("Create an account", "Customize", "Launch"); or the same numbered treatment is repeated across several sections. In the HTML/CSS source: a grid of 3-4 children rendered from an array with fields step/number, title, description; elements containing only "1", "2", "3" or "01", "02", "03" set in large or bold type or inside rounded-full badges; "How it works" as the section heading; an absolutely positioned connector line between steps. Does not count: a real procedure the visitor must follow with concrete, product-specific steps (installation commands, an application process with documents and dates, a recipe); a timeline with dates; an ordered list inside running text; a checkout progress indicator. Describe the visible pattern only; do not infer how the page was made.

positive: Section 'How it works' with three equal cards, each topped by a purple circle containing 1, 2 or 3, titled 'Sign up', 'Customize', 'Launch', each with one generic sentence, joined by a dashed line.

patterns.legitimate_use: Real, product-specific procedures where order matters and each step contains information the visitor needs to act on, and timelines whose markers carry real dates.
patterns.fix: If the items are not a sequence, remove the numbers and treat them as content of their own (or fold them into the feature they describe). If they are a real process, make each step concrete: what the visitor actually does, what they need, how long it takes, ideally with a screenshot or example, and drop steps that state the obvious.
patterns.prevention: Number items only when the order carries information the visitor needs. Before writing a "How it works" section, check that the steps are specific to this product or service and that someone could follow them; otherwise show the process with a real example, a short demo or a single sentence. Do not reuse the same 01/02/03 treatment across sections. An explicit brand or user wish overrides this.

patterns.name: Purple-blue gradient default
patterns.summary: The page's accent is an indigo, violet or purple hue, usually as a gradient into blue, pink or cyan, spread across hero background, primary buttons and highlights, while nothing in the brand or subject calls for it. Both major model vendors name purple gradients on white as a default their models fall into, three independent design skills ban it as the most recognizable tell, and the Tailwind CSS creator joked that his indigo-500 buttons turned generated interfaces indigo.

detector.rubric: Look at the hero, the primary call-to-action buttons and the main accent color across the page. Flag the page when its dominant accent is indigo, violet or purple and appears as a gradient into blue, pink, magenta or cyan (or as flat indigo/violet buttons and highlights paired with such a gradient elsewhere) on the hero background, buttons, badges or section washes, and the page shows no brand reason for the hue (no logo, product or imagery in that hue). Count one hit per page. When only the source is available, signs are Tailwind pairs such as from-indigo-500/from-purple-600/from-violet-500 with to-blue-*/to-pink-*/to-cyan-*, bg-indigo-500 or bg-violet-600 on the main button, or CSS like linear-gradient(135deg, #667eea, #764ba2). patterns.name: Stat banner row
patterns.summary: A band or hero block of three to six big numbers with small labels ("10K+ users", "99.9% uptime", "24/7 support", "4.9 stars") is inserted as a stock section, usually evenly spaced in a row or in matching tiles, often with a gradient accent on the figures. It fills space and signals scale without connecting to the page's argument. A DOM-based corpus scan of Show HN landing pages scored "Stat banner rows" as one of its layout patterns, and Anthropic's design skill calls "a big number with a small label, supporting stats, and a gradient accent" "the default treatment".

detector.rubric: Flag a section (one hit per page is enough) that consists mainly of 3 to 6 sibling items laid out in a row or equal tiles, where each item's dominant element is a short large figure (a number with K, M, %, x, +, a star rating or "24/7", at most about ten characters, clearly larger than the body text) with a small label under or beside it, and where the figures are not explained, sourced or connected to a nearby argument. Also flag a hero whose main element is one big number with a small label plus a row of supporting stats. Round or maximal figures (10K+, 99.9%, 100+, 24/7, 5x) strengthen the hit. In the HTML/CSS source: a flex or grid container (grid-cols-2 md:grid-cols-4) of 3-6 children, each with a text-4xl/5xl font-bold element holding a short numeric string and a text-sm muted label, sometimes animated with a count-up script or gradient text (bg-clip-text). Does not count: prices in a pricing table; numbered step markers (1, 2, 3 or 01, 02, 03); a data visualization or table of real metrics with dates and sources; a single figure inside a sentence; dashboards or reports whose purpose is numbers. Whether the figures are true is judged by other patterns; this one judges the stock component. Describe the visible pattern only; do not infer how the page was made.

positive: Below the hero, a full-width tinted band with four evenly spaced figures in large gradient type: '10K+ Active users', '99.9% Uptime', '24/7 Support', '150+ Countries', each with a small gray label and nothing else.

Hero of a consulting firm whose main element is a huge '500+' with the small label 'clients served', followed by a row of three smaller stats ('98% satisfaction', '15 years', '3x ROI') in matching rounded tiles.
Four equal cards near the footer of a craft-brewery site reading '50K+', '4.9/5', '100%', '24/7' with one-word labels.
negative: Annual-report page with a chart of yearly revenue and a sourced table of figures by quarter.
Pricing table with three plans showing '$0', '$12' and '$29' per month.
How-it-works section with three steps labeled 1, 2 and 3.

patterns.legitimate_use: Real, specific figures that matter to the visitor and are explained where they appear (a charity's audited results with year and source, a transit system's on-time rate with a link to the data), shown in a form chosen for that content.
patterns.fix: Delete the band unless the figures are real, specific and relevant; if they are, attach each one to the claim it supports, give period and source, and present it where it argues something (in the feature it proves, in a chart, in a sentence) instead of in a free-floating row.
patterns.prevention: Do not add a row of big round numbers as a section by default. Use a figure only when it is real, specific and meaningful to the visitor, place it next to the claim it supports with its period and source, and choose a presentation that fits the data (a sentence, a chart, a table). Open the page with the subject itself rather than a big-number hero unless the number is the story. An explicit brand or user wish overrides this.

patterns.name: Stock "tasteful" palette
patterns.summary: The page avoids the purple default by landing on one of the next stock looks: warm cream or beige paper with a high-contrast (often italic) serif display and a terracotta or clay accent, or a near-black page with a single bright neon accent (acid green, vermilion, cyan). Anthropic's own design skill lists both as traits generated design "clusters around", and two further design skills flag the cream palette, the italic serif hero and neon-on-dark as defaults models reach for.

detector.rubric: Look at the page background, the display typeface and the accent color together. Flag the page when it matches one of two looks and nothing in the subject or brand motivates it: (a) a warm off-white, cream or beige page background, a high-contrast or italic serif for the headline, and a terracotta, rust, clay or burnt-orange accent; (b) a near-black or tinted-black background with one bright neon accent (acid green, lime, vermilion, electric cyan) used for buttons, highlights and small labels, often with monospace labels. Count one hit per page. When only the source is available, signs are background values near #F4F1EA, #FAF9F5 or similar warm off-whites with an accent near #D97757 or #C96442 and a serif display family (Fraunces, Instrument Serif, Playfair Display, Newsreader, Recoleta); or a background of #0B0B0B, #111 or similar with a single accent like #C6FF00, #D4FF3F or #FF4D00. Does not count: brands whose identity is these colors (a bakery whose packaging is cream and terracotta, a sports brand with a neon-green logo); editorial and magazine sites where a serif on paper is the genre; developer tools that use a dark theme with a syntax-highlighting accent tied to the product; the purple-blue default (see purple-blue-gradient-default). Describe the visible pattern only; do not infer how the page was made.

positive: Landing page for a cloud backup service on a cream background, with a large italic serif headline and terracotta buttons and underlines; the product's logo is blue.
Near-black page for an HR tool with a single acid-green accent on the buttons, the headline highlight and small monospace labels.
Agency template with beige paper texture, a high-contrast serif display, clay-colored links and hairline rules, used for a cybersecurity product.
negative: Website of a pottery studio whose real glazes and clay are shown in photos, with a cream background and a terracotta accent drawn from them.
Literary magazine site using a serif on off-white because it reproduces its printed issues.
Sports drink site with a neon-green accent taken from its can design on a black background.

patterns.legitimate_use: Brands, subjects and genres that own these colors and faces (craft, food, print media, a neon brand mark), or a brief that asks for the look. The pattern is reaching for it as the safe alternative when the axis is free.
patterns.fix: Move at least one axis away from the stock look, starting with the accent: take the accent from the product or brand, then reconsider the background, then the display face. Check that the result still fits the subject.
patterns.prevention: Derive background, display face and accent from the subject: its materials, places, printed matter and brand assets. Write down why each was chosen. When the brief leaves color and type free, do not settle on cream paper with a serif and a clay accent, or on near-black with one neon accent, as the "distinctive" choice; pick from the subject's world instead.

patterns.name: Template centered hero stack
patterns.summary: The first screen is a single centered column: a small pill badge, a large headline, a gray subheadline, and one or two buttons (filled primary, outlined or ghost secondary), often with a framed product screenshot or dashboard mock below. The same stack appears whatever the page is for, so the opening says nothing about the subject. A corpus scan of about 1,500 Show HN landing pages used "Centered hero set in a generic sans" and "Badge right above the hero H1" as two of its checks, and several practitioner write-ups describe the same centered headline, badge and button pair as the default.

detector.rubric: Look at the first viewport only. Flag the page when the hero is a horizontally centered stack with no competing element beside it and contains at least three of these four parts in this vertical order: (1) a small rounded pill or chip above the headline (text such as "New", "Now in beta", "Introducing ...", a version number or "Backed by ...", often with a sparkle, dot or arrow); (2) a large centered headline of one to three lines; (3) a centered, lighter or gray subheadline paragraph; (4) a row of one or two centered buttons, typically one filled and one outlined, ghost or text-with-arrow. A framed screenshot, browser chrome or dashboard mock centered directly beneath strengthens the hit but is not required. One hit per page. In the HTML/CSS source: a first section whose wrapper uses text-center / text-align:center or flex-col items-center with mx-auto max-w-*; a rounded-full inline element with small text before the h1; a paragraph with a muted text color (text-gray-500/600, text-muted-foreground) after it; and a flex row of two links or buttons with different variants (default and outline). Does not count: a left-aligned or split hero (text on one side, image or demo on the other); a centered hero whose main element is a full-bleed photograph, video, live product, interactive demo or typographic composition that carries the subject; a centered page title on an inner page (docs, blog post, legal); an event or campaign page whose badge carries real information (date and venue) and whose layout is otherwise subject-specific. Describe the visible pattern only; do not infer how the page was made.

positive: Landing page for an invoicing tool: on a white background, centered, a small rounded chip reading 'New: AI reminders' with a sparkle icon, under it a two-line bold headline, a gray one-sentence subheadline, then two buttons side by side, a solid 'Start free trial' and an outlined 'Book a demo'; below, a tilted screenshot of a dashboard in a rounded frame.

Site for a local bakery whose first screen is a centered pill 'Now taking online orders', a large headline, a gray subtitle, and the buttons 'Order now' and 'Learn more', with no photograph of bread or of the shop anywhere in the first viewport.

Dark developer-tool page: a centered pill 'v2.0 is here ->', a big headline, a muted gray subheadline, a filled 'Get started' button next to a ghost 'View on GitHub' button, and a terminal-window mock centered underneath.
negative: Hero with the headline and one button left-aligned in the left half and a large product photograph filling the right half.
Centered hero of a museum exhibition page consisting of a full-bleed photograph of the main exhibit with the exhibition title overlaid and the dates as the only small label.
Documentation start page with a centered search field and title 'How can we help?' and no buttons or badge.

patterns.legitimate_use: A centered stack is a sound choice for a single-action page (a waitlist, an app download) when the content is deliberately minimal and the type, imagery or demo inside it is specific to the product; a badge is legitimate when it carries real, current news.
patterns.fix: Decide what the most characteristic thing in the subject's world is and lead with it: the real product in use, a photograph of the place, a live demo, a strong typographic statement. Move the text off the center axis or into a split composition when the visual needs the space, keep one primary action, and delete the badge unless it states a concrete, current fact.
patterns.prevention: Do not open with the badge-headline-subheadline-two-buttons stack by reflex. Before building the hero, name the one thing a visitor must see first (product, place, people, result) and compose the first screen around it: choose alignment deliberately (left, split, asymmetric or centered for a reason), give it one clear primary action, and use real screenshots or photographs instead of a generic dashboard frame. An explicit brand or user wish overrides this.

patterns.name: Template landing-page section sequence
patterns.summary: The page is assembled from the stock landing-page kit in its stock order: hero, logo strip or social proof, feature grid, how-it-works steps, testimonials, a three-tier pricing table with a raised middle plan, an FAQ accordion, a closing call-to-action band and a multi-column footer, whatever the site is for. The sequence comes from component-library examples and templates, not from the content, so a bakery, a nonprofit and a developer tool get the same page. A developer who asked three code-generation tools for a landing page got this order "practically identical" each time, design reviewers of vibe-coded sites name the same run of sections, and a preprint on vibe coding describes "generic layouts" produced "regardless of the cultural context".

detector.rubric: Judge the full-page screenshot as a whole. List the sections from top to bottom and match them against the stock kit: (a) centered hero; (b) logo strip or "Trusted by" row; (c) grid of 3, 4 or 6 feature cards; (d) numbered "How it works" steps; (e) testimonial cards or carousel; (f) pricing table of three plans side by side with the middle one highlighted, raised or labeled "Most popular"; (g) FAQ accordion near the bottom; (h) full-width closing CTA band; (i) footer with three to five link columns. Flag the page (one hit) when at least five of the nine kit sections are present and they appear in this relative order, and when at least one present section does not fit what the site offers (for example a pricing table or "trusted by" logos on a site that sells nothing per seat, an FAQ with generic questions) or when no section exists that is specific to the subject (a menu, a map, a schedule, a portfolio, a reading list). In the HTML/CSS source: sibling <section> elements with ids or headings such as #features, #how-it-works, #testimonials, #pricing, #faq, #cta, often each wrapped in the same container (max-w-7xl mx-auto px-6 py-24); a pricing grid of three cards where one has a 'Most popular' badge, a ring/border-primary or scale-105; <details> or accordion components in the lower half. Does not count: a software product page that has a real pricing model, real customers and real FAQs and also includes sections specific to the product (changelog, docs, integrations list, live demo); a page with only two or three of the kit sections; a page that uses the same section types in an order and form driven by its content (for example pricing first on a page for existing customers). Describe the visible pattern only; do not infer how the page was made.

positive: Page for a family-run dental practice that scrolls through: centered hero, a row of grayscale 'trusted by' logos, six feature cards ('Fast', 'Secure', 'Friendly'), three numbered steps, three testimonial cards, three price plans with the middle one marked 'Most popular', an FAQ accordion, a gradient band 'Ready to get started?' and a four-column footer; no team photos, opening hours or map.

Portfolio site of an illustrator built as hero, feature grid ('Creative', 'Reliable', 'Fast delivery'), how-it-works steps, testimonials, three pricing tiers, FAQ and closing CTA, with only one small image of the artist's work.

Community garden association page with hero, 'Trusted by' row, feature cards, testimonials, three membership plans with a highlighted middle plan labeled 'Most popular', FAQ accordion and CTA band, in that order.
negative: Software product page with hero, real customer logos, feature sections that each show a real screenshot, an integrations directory, a changelog link, pricing with a usage calculator and a contact form.
Restaurant site with a full-bleed photo hero, the menu, opening hours with a map, a reservation widget and an Instagram strip.
A pricing page whose whole purpose is comparing plans, with a feature comparison table and FAQ about billing.

patterns.legitimate_use: Software and subscription products with a real tiered price, real customers and recurring questions can legitimately use these sections; the sequence is a reasonable default when each section carries real, product-specific content and sections without content are left out.
patterns.fix: Write down what a visitor to this specific site needs to do or know, in order, and rebuild the page from that list. Delete sections without real content (logos of non-customers, generic FAQs, pricing on a site that sells nothing per plan), add the sections the subject needs (menu, map, schedule, case studies, portfolio), and vary section form and rhythm instead of stacking identical containers.
patterns.prevention: Do not start from the hero-features-steps-testimonials-pricing-FAQ-CTA kit. Derive the page structure from the subject: list the visitor's questions and the content you actually have, then order and shape sections around them (for a place: location, hours, what it looks like; for a portfolio: the work; for a nonprofit: what it does and how to help). Include pricing, testimonials and FAQ only when real content exists, and give at least one section a form that only this site would have. An explicit brand or user wish overrides this.

patterns.name: Unconfigured framework defaults in the source
patterns.summary: The styling uses a utility framework exactly as shipped: every color is a stock palette step (indigo-600, slate-900, gray-500), spacing, radius and shadow are stock scale steps, there is no project theme or token layer, and the same long utility string is pasted onto every repeated element instead of a component or class. The source shows that no design system was set up, which is why such pages look interchangeable. Tailwind's creator attributes the indigo look of generated UIs to the bg-indigo-500 default in Tailwind UI; a component vendor describes LLM output that rebuilds each button from raw utilities so that "One button becomes five different button class strings"; a practitioner checklist names default palette steps such as gray-900.

detector.rubric: Needs the HTML/JSX/CSS source (and tailwind config or CSS theme block if present). Flag one hit per page when all three hold: (1) Colors: every or nearly every color utility uses a stock framework palette name with a numeric step (bg-indigo-600, hover:bg-indigo-700, text-gray-600, text-slate-500, bg-gray-50, from-purple-600 to-blue-500, Bootstrap btn-primary with stock blue), and there is no custom color token (bg-brand, text-primary, var(--color-accent), a theme extension, arbitrary hex values chosen for the brand). (2) No theme: no tailwind.config theme extension, no @theme block or CSS custom properties defining the palette, fonts or radii, or the config exists but is empty. (3) Repetition: the same long utility string (about 8 or more classes, e.g. "rounded-xl bg-white p-6 shadow-md hover:shadow-lg transition") is copied verbatim on three or more sibling elements, or near-identical strings with small arbitrary differences (p-6 here, p-8 there) style what is visually the same component. Does not count: a project that defines its own tokens even if they are mapped to framework scales (primary: colors.indigo); shadcn/ui or similar setups that use semantic variables (bg-primary, text-muted-foreground) from a theme file; repetition produced by a loop or component (one class string in a map() or a Card component); prototypes, docs examples or internal tools labelled as such; a single default color among custom tokens. Describe the visible pattern only; do not infer how the page was made.

Three pricing cards, each written out by hand with the identical string class="bg-white rounded-2xl shadow-lg p-8 border border-gray-100 hover:shadow-xl transition-all duration-300 transform hover:-translate-y-1".

patterns.legitimate_use: Stock framework palettes are well designed and fine for prototypes, internal tools, admin screens and documentation examples, or when the brand color happens to match a default step and is aliased as a token. The pattern is a public-facing page whose whole visual language is the unmodified kit.
patterns.fix: Define a small token set (4-6 named colors, a type scale, one or two radii, one shadow) in the framework theme or as CSS custom properties, replace stock palette names with those tokens, and extract repeated utility strings into a component or a single class. Then adjust the tokens to the brand instead of editing class strings one by one.
patterns.prevention: Before writing markup, set up the theme: name the brand colors, fonts, radii and shadow as tokens and use only those names in the markup; reach for stock palette steps only for neutral utility (borders, disabled states) and only through an alias. Build each repeated element once as a component. Choose the accent from the subject and brand, not from the framework's example buttons. An explicit brand or user wish (e.g. "use stock Tailwind") overrides this.

patterns.name: Unfilled page placeholders and template defaults
patterns.summary: A published page still carries the stand-in content of its template or generator: lorem ipsum, "Your Company" or Acme as the site's own name, example.com addresses and 555 phone numbers, links and social icons that point to "#", a copyright line with an old year, and the framework's default page title or favicon. The generator fills every slot with plausible dummy values when the brief has none, and nobody replaces them. Launch checklists for AI-built sites list these strings and dead links as typical leftovers, a scan of 100 showcase sites from AI site builders found default favicons and stale copyright years, and Anthropic's design skill notes that the model often has to come up with "placeholder content" itself.

detector.rubric: Read the page's HTML/JSX source together with its visible text. Strong signals (any one is a hit): lorem ipsum or other filler Latin; the site's own name or contact block given as "Your Company", "Company Name", "Brand", "Acme" or a bracketed slot; staff or author names "John Doe" / "Jane Doe"; contact data on reserved or dummy values (an example.com or example.org address, "you@company.com", "info@businessname.com", a 555 phone number, "123 Main Street"); visible "TODO", "Coming soon" or "Image here" text in a shipped section. Weak signals (two different kinds together are a hit): three or more navigation, footer or call-to-action links with href="#" or "javascript:void(0)" and no click handler; social icons linking to "#" or to a platform's home page instead of a profile; a hard-coded copyright year earlier than the previous calendar year; a <title> left at a framework or tool default ("Vite + React", "React App", "Create Next App") or the same title on every page; the framework's default favicon (for example vite.svg, the default favicon.ico of a starter); image sources pointing to placeholder services or files (placeholder.svg, placehold.co, via.placeholder.com). Count one hit per page. Does not count: documentation, tutorials or code samples that use example.com or 555 numbers as examples on purpose; template or theme demo pages sold or shown as templates; form placeholder attributes ("you@example.com" as the hint inside an email input); href="#" on elements that are wired to a script (tabs, menus), which is a markup issue, not a placeholder; a copyright year from the previous year early in the new year; a page explicitly labelled as a prototype or staging build. The bracketed-slot form inside prose is the text pattern unfilled-placeholder; this pattern is the page-level template residue. Describe the visible pattern only; do not infer how the page was made.

patterns.name: Uniform decorative motion
patterns.summary: The same entrance and hover effects are applied to everything regardless of purpose: every section fades and slides up on scroll, every card scales or lifts on hover, numbers count up, headlines type themselves, backgrounds float or follow the cursor, often with transition-all and without a prefers-reduced-motion fallback. Motion that is not triggered by the user and does not explain a change adds load and distraction. Anthropic's design skill calls "fade-and-slide-up entrances on each section and hover transitions on every card" the generic default; reviewers of vibe-coded sites list automatic fade-ins, superfluous background animation and purposeless hover movement; Vercel's agent guidelines forbid transition: all and require honoring reduced motion.

detector.rubric: Read the source (HTML/JSX classes, CSS, animation libraries such as AOS, framer-motion, GSAP, IntersectionObserver code). Flag one hit per page when motion is applied uniformly: (a) a scroll-reveal (fade-in, fade-up, data-aos, whileInView, an observer adding a class) on most sections or most cards, AND at least one of (b) the same hover transform on most cards or buttons (hover:scale-105, hover:-translate-y-1, whileHover scale), (c) decorative non-interactive animation (counting-up statistics, typewriter headline, floating or pulsing blobs, cursor-follow light, infinite marquee), (d) transition-all / transition: all on many elements. Add a note, not a second hit, when there is no prefers-reduced-motion media query or useReducedMotion check. If only a screenshot or the rendered page is available, judge it by scrolling: the same entrance on every block and the same lift on every card. Does not count: one orchestrated hero or page-load sequence; motion that responds to a user action and shows a state change (menu opening, accordion expanding, toast, button press feedback); hover color or underline changes; a single hover lift used only on clickable cards that link somewhere; a product demo or animation that is the content; motion wrapped in a reduced-motion guard and limited to one or two places. Describe the visible pattern only; do not infer how the page was made.

positive: Every <section> has data-aos="fade-up", every feature card has class="transition-all duration-300 hover:scale-105 hover:shadow-xl", and the stats row animates from 0 to '10,000+' on scroll; no prefers-reduced-motion rule in the CSS.
document.querySelectorAll('section').forEach(s => observer.observe(s)) adding 'animate-fade-in-up' to each section, plus a hero headline that types itself letter by letter with a blinking cursor.

<motion.div initial={{opacity:0,y:40}} whileInView={{opacity:1,y:0}} whileHover={{scale:1.05}}> wrapped around each of twelve cards, testimonials and pricing tiers, and two blurred gradient blobs with animate-pulse floating behind the hero.
negative: A hero with one staggered page-load sequence (headline, then subline, then CTA), all other sections static, wrapped in @media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference).
Navigation drawer that slides in when the menu button is pressed and an accordion whose panel expands with a height transition.
Link cards that change border color and underline the title on hover, using transition-colors only.

patterns.legitimate_use: Motion is legitimate when it answers a user action, explains a change of state, or is the product itself (an animation studio, a demo of an interactive tool). One deliberate entrance moment can carry a brand. The pattern is the same effect stamped on every block.
patterns.fix: Remove scroll reveals from all sections except, at most, one moment that matters; drop hover transforms from non-clickable elements and keep a subtle color or border change on clickable ones; replace transition-all with the specific properties (opacity, transform, color); remove counters and typing effects or show the final value; wrap remaining motion in a prefers-reduced-motion guard.
patterns.prevention: Decide where motion carries meaning before adding any: feedback for user actions, state changes, and at most one orchestrated entrance. Animate only opacity and transform, name the properties instead of "all", and always provide a reduced-motion variant. Show numbers and headlines in their final state. An explicit brand or user wish for a motion-heavy experience overrides this, but still honor reduced motion.

patterns.name: Uniform rounded-card surface kit
patterns.summary: Every container on the page wears the same surface recipe regardless of hierarchy: one generous corner radius, the same soft low-opacity drop shadow, often a hairline border under that shadow, and the same hover lift or scale on every card. The look matches the stock settings of popular component kits. Anthropic's design skill calls it "the SaaS-card kit", two further design skills check for the hairline border under a wide shadow and identical hover lifts, and an HCI preprint names "standard drop shadows or rounded corners" as the generic styles that override a brand.

detector.rubric: Judge surface styling only, not how the cards are arranged. Look at cards, panels, buttons, inputs, images and badges across the page. Flag the page when nearly all containers share one large corner radius (roughly 12 to 24px) and one soft, diffuse, low-contrast shadow, with no variation between levels (a page-level panel, a card inside it and a button all rounded alike), especially when a 1px light-grey border sits under a wide soft shadow, or when every card lifts, scales or gains a bigger shadow on hover in the same way. Count one hit per page. When only the source is available, signs are the same rounded-xl or rounded-2xl plus shadow-sm/shadow-md/shadow-lg plus border on most container elements, CSS like border-radius: 12px with box-shadow: 0 1px 3px rgba(0,0,0,.1) or 0 20px 60px rgba(0,0,0,.1) repeated across selectors, and hover:-translate-y-1, hover:scale-105 or hover:shadow-xl on every card. Does not count: a product UI built on a documented design system whose radius and elevation tokens are applied consistently with real hierarchy (modals elevated, inline cards flat); rounded shapes that come from the brand (a pill-shaped logo language, a children's brand); a single floating element (a modal, a popover) that has both border and shadow; hover feedback on genuinely interactive elements that differs by element type. Describe the visible pattern only; do not infer how the page was made.

positive: Landing page where the hero panel, the six feature cards, the testimonial cards, the pricing cards and the newsletter box all have the same 16px rounded corners, a thin light-grey border and the same faint wide shadow.
Page on which every card, including non-clickable info boxes, rises a few pixels and grows its shadow on hover.
Rounded white cards with soft grey shadows nested inside a larger rounded white panel with the same radius and the same shadow.
negative: A banking app where only the modal dialog floats with a shadow and a border, while list rows and cards are flat with hairline dividers.
A toy store site whose bubbly rounded shapes repeat the rounded letterforms of its logo and packaging.
A brutalist portfolio with square corners and a hard black offset shadow chosen as the page's concept.

patterns.legitimate_use: Application interfaces built on a design system where shared tokens are the point and elevation follows hierarchy; brands whose identity is soft and rounded; a single elevated element that needs both edge and depth.
patterns.fix: Define a surface ladder: plain whitespace first, then a hairline divider, then a tinted well, then a card only for content that is independently interactive. Give each nesting level its own radius (smaller inside), use either a border or a shadow but not both, drop decorative shadows, and keep one hover signal per interactive element type.
patterns.prevention: Derive shape and depth from the brand and the content: decide a radius scale (it may be zero) and use it by level, separate most content with spacing, type and dividers rather than boxes, reserve shadows for things that actually float, and give hover feedback only to interactive elements, with one signal each. Do not ship a component kit's stock radius, shadow and hover-lift settings unchanged.

patterns.name: Unsourced round proof metrics and badges
patterns.summary: Customer counts, satisfaction rates, uptime, speed multipliers, ratings, rankings and award seals are stated as facts on the page with no source, date or issuer: "50,000+ happy customers", "99.9% uptime", "10x faster", "#1 rated". The numbers fill the proof slot of the page template rather than report anything measured. Launch checklists for AI-built sites list made-up badges and numbers ("Trusted by 2,000 teams", "500+ happy clients", "trusted by 10,000 teams") as a typical defect, and design reviewers of vibe-coded startup sites said a row of 10x claims "just feels made up".

detector.rubric: Look at the hero, stat bands, badges, feature claims and footer for quantitative or ranking claims about the business: number of customers, users, teams or downloads; satisfaction or success percentages; uptime; time or money saved; speed or growth multipliers; average ratings; ranks ("#1", "top-rated", "leading"); award or "certified" seals. Flag the page when at least one such claim is presented as fact with no visible source and has at least one of these forms: a round or plus-suffixed figure ("10K+", "50,000+", "500+ clients"), a percentage or multiplier of benefit ("99.9%", "98% satisfaction", "3x conversions", "10x faster"), a rating without a named platform and review count, a superlative rank, or a badge or seal with no named issuer and year. A visible source means a footnote, a link (status page, review platform, report), a named issuer with date, or a named customer case. Count one hit per page, however many stats there are. Judge the claim, not the layout of the stat band. From source only: hard-coded stats arrays ({value: "10K+", label: "Active users"}) or count-up animation components fed with constants. Does not count: product specifications (file-size limits, supported languages, price, response time of a documented SLA linked from the page); plain business facts (year founded, number of rooms, opening hours); ratings with platform, review count and date; figures attributed to a named customer case study; numbers in a clearly hypothetical calculator. Describe the visible pattern only; do not infer how the page was made.

positive: A stat band under the hero on a just-launched tool: '10K+ Active users', '99.9% Uptime', '4.9/5 Average rating', '24/7 Support', in large gradient numerals, with no source, review platform or status page link anywhere.
Hero badge 'Trusted by 2,000+ teams' with a row of overlapping avatar circles, on a page whose pricing section says the product is in early access.
Feature section claiming '10x faster deployments', '3x more conversions' and '#1 rated platform' with a gold laurel seal reading 'Award winning 2026' and no named award or issuer.
negative: '4.7 on a named review platform, 1,284 reviews, updated October 2026', linking to the platform's listing.
'Uptime last 90 days: 99.95%' linking to a public status page with incident history.
A guesthouse page stating 'Fourteen rooms, family-run since 1987, 300 m from the beach'.

patterns.legitimate_use: Measured, sourced figures; business facts the owner supplies; awards with a named issuer and year; case-study results attributed to a named customer.
patterns.fix: Delete every figure, rating, rank and badge that the owner cannot back with a source. Keep the numbers that are true and add their source (platform and date, status page, report, named customer). If nothing remains, remove the stat band and use the space to show what the product does.
patterns.prevention: Never invent numbers, ratings, rankings or award badges. Use only figures from the brief or the owner's data, written precisely and with their source next to them. With no figures, describe the product concretely (what a user uploads, clicks and gets) or show a real screenshot instead of a stat band.

patterns.name: Placeholder or unverified "trusted by" logo wall
patterns.summary: A "Trusted by" or "Used by teams at" strip is filled with logos that cannot stand for real customers: placeholder names (Acme), invented wordmarks made of a stock icon plus one generic word, or well-known brand names typed as plain text. The strip is a standard section of the landing-page template, so it gets filled even when no customer exists. Launch checklists for AI-built sites name "logos of companies you never worked with" and "placeholder logos still sitting in the bar" as typical defects and tell owners to search for "Acme".

detector.rubric: Find the logo strip or grid that presents customers, users, partners or press ("Trusted by", "Used by teams at", "Powering", "As seen in", or an unlabelled row of logos under the hero). Flag it when the logos show one of these: (1) placeholder or stock-fictional names (Acme, Globex, Initech, "Company", "Logo", "Brand", "Logoipsum"); (2) invented generic wordmarks: a simple icon glyph (hexagon, bolt, triangle, circle, leaf) next to one generic word (Nexus, Vertex, Quantum, Lumina, Apex, Stellar) in the page's own typeface, often five or six of them in identical weight and gray; (3) names of globally known brands set as plain text in one uniform font instead of their actual marks. Count one hit per page. From source only: the logos are text spans or icon-library glyphs from an array of names rather than image or SVG brand assets; alt texts like "Company 1"; file names like logo-1.svg with generic shapes. Does not count: real brand marks as image assets (even if the relationship cannot be verified from the page; do not guess); integration or compatibility rows ("Works with", "Connects to") that show tools the product integrates with; certification or payment-method badges; a press strip linking to the articles; a template demo that labels its logos as sample. Describe the visible pattern only; do not infer how the page was made.

positive: Under the hero, gray text 'Trusted by innovative teams worldwide' and six gray wordmarks: a hexagon with 'Nexus', a bolt with 'Voltix', a triangle with 'Apex', a circle with 'Lumina', a leaf with 'Verde', a star with 'Stellar', all in the page's sans-serif at the same weight.

Logo bar on a newly launched app reading 'Used by teams at' followed by the names of five of the world's largest technology companies typed in plain bold text in the page font, no logos and no case studies anywhere on the page.
A row labelled 'Our clients' showing 'ACME', 'Acme Corp', 'Globex' and 'Company' as light gray text blocks.
negative: A 'Works with' row showing the official icons of the chat, calendar and storage services the product integrates with, each linking to an integration docs page.
A strip of distinct customer brand marks as image files, each different in shape and color, with a 'Read the case study' link under two of them.
A row of payment-method and security-certification badges above the checkout button.

patterns.legitimate_use: Real customer or press logos used with permission; integration rows; template demos that label their sample logos.
patterns.fix: Remove every logo that does not stand for a real customer, partner or publication that agreed to appear. If real ones exist, use their actual brand assets with permission and link at least one to a case study or article. If none exist, delete the strip and use the space for something the page can prove: a product screenshot, a concrete example, a founder note.
patterns.prevention: Never invent company names, wordmarks or logos, and never list real brands the brief does not name as customers. Build a logo strip only from logos the owner supplies, as their real assets; with none, leave the section out and show the product itself in that space. An explicit brand or user wish overrides this only with real material.
